#5452. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

#5451. Inside a Secluded Cabin Hidden Right Beneath Big Sur’s Iconic Landmark

A secluded retreat tucked beneath one of California’s most photographed landmarks in Big Sur has come on the market for $3.65 million.

The home at 39320 Coast Road sits in Bixby Canyon and is one of only seven residences behind a private gate.

“Millions recognize Bixby Bridge, yet very few will ever experience the landscape beneath it,” says listing agent Michael Hornig of the Strock Team at eXp Realty.

The canyon also comes with a literary history: In 1960, Jack Kerouac retreated to a cabin here owned by Lawrence Ferlinghetti, the poet and co-founder of City Lights Bookstore. His time in the canyon formed the basis for his 1962 novel, “Big Sur.” While this is not the original Kerouac cabin, it shares the same setting.

According to Hornig, the canyon has also been home to the film director Sam Peckinpah and the Disney illustrator Ron Dias.

“There’s an extraordinary feeling about this canyon,” Hornig says. “You’re surrounded by a landscape that inspired some of America’s most influential writers, and remarkably, much of that atmosphere of solitude and wilderness remains intact today.”

Built in 1984, the single-level home has three bedrooms, two full bathrooms, and 1,489 square feet of living space. Vaulted, open-beam ceilings, hardwood floors, and three wood-burning stoves characterize the interiors, as do large windows that frame the surrounding redwoods. A wraparound porch overlooks the forest.

“Luxury doesn’t always have to be expressed through scale or elaborate architecture,” Hornig says. “Here, the luxury is the relationship between the home and its surroundings.”

The property covers two parcels: a 0.79-acre residential lot and an adjacent 0.33-acre creekside lot. It is move-in ready, with a private well, septic system, and electricity. There is also a fenced backyard, storage shed, pasture space and parking for 10 vehicles, including EV charging.

Owners share access to a privately held canyon enclave of more than 140 acres. There, a creekside trail winds through redwoods and ferns to a secluded beach beneath the bridge.

“You can walk from your front door through a redwood forest, follow the creek toward the Pacific, and emerge beneath one of the most recognizable bridges in the world,” Hornig says.

Next to the property, Brazil Ranch adds about 1,200 acres of U.S. Forest Service land for hiking, hunting, and recreation. The historic Old Coast Road offers miles of biking, horseback riding, and backcountry exploration. Highway 1 is about five minutes away. Carmel, Monterey, and Big Sur’s restaurants and state parks are about 20 minutes away.

“To me, the greatest luxury here is the privilege of belonging to a landscape that most people will only ever admire from a distance,” Hornig says. "It's this contrast between one of California’s most recognizable landmarks and the hidden residential community beneath it."

Larissa Runkle is a seasoned real estate writer, lifestyle journalist, and marketing strategist with over a decade of experience and 2,000+ published articles. Her work covering housing, personal finance, and lifestyle has appeared in major publications like Bankrate, MarketWatch, Yahoo Finance, and New York Post. In 2023, she launched a boutique copywriting studio to partner with land developers and top brokerages, creating strategic content that builds lasting brand authority. When she isn’t writing, Larissa enjoys the outdoors from her home in the San Juan Mountains of Colorado, where she lives with her husband, son, and German shepherd, Yoko.

#5450. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

#5449. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

Social media platforms allow you to connect directly with your target audience too. You can answer queries and concerns in your DMs and show the human side of your brand.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

Optimize your videos for search engines by including keywords and phrases in your video titles and descriptions. Doing so increases your rankings on SERPs and puts your brand in front of as many people as possible.

#5448. Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

Popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

Studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

More definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

"We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit," says Stina Börchers.

Unlocking New Treatments to Protect Memory

A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

"Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

They also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain.

#5447. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:

First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:

The first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

As seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer says deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision.  At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

Google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

Now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

That said, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:

Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

Coming back to the AI inference issue. As we showed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract says.”

This means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

For sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

In this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:

We see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

This means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

For vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

Sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Join theCUBE’s Alumni Trust Network, where technology leaders connect, share intelligence and create opportunities.

Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals. Our new proprietary theCUBE AI Video Cloud is breaking ground in audience interaction, leveraging theCUBEai.com neural network to help technology companies make data-driven decisions and stay at the forefront of industry conversations.

#5446. Rare 25-Foot-Wide Carnegie Hill Townhouse With a Private Carriage House Lists for $11.95 Million

A 25-foot-wide townhouse with a carriage house has just hit the market for $11.95 million in Manhattan’s Carnegie Hill.

Built in 1899, the five-bedroom residence underwent a “no-expense-spared” reconstruction and features 13 newly renovated rooms, each with individually zoned heating and cooling.

“It is certainly very rare for a listing like this townhouse with a carriage house to come on the market in uptown Manhattan,” said listing agent Daniella G. Schlisser of Brown Harris Stevens. “I don’t recall ever seeing something like this here.”

The 7,700-square-foot interior was entirely gutted and rebuilt with new structural steel, plumbing, electrical, and commercial-grade mechanical systems.

“It has incredible sun and light, which is incredibly unusual for a townhouse,” Schlisser said. “The home is flooded with direct sunlight facing the back and it also gets sun to the north in the front.”

The six-story dwelling features a garden level that leads to a limestone gallery with custom paneling. There is a separately accessed commercial space offering “continued retail or office use” that could also be transformed into additional living space. French doors open to a bluestone-decked garden with a built-in grill.

“There is a phenomenal amount of space and light, and being a 25-foot-wide townhouse is also rare,” she noted.

A parlor level boasts a living room with a fireplace and herringbone floors. The nearby formal dining room was designed for grand-scale entertaining. Also on this level is a garden-facing eat-in kitchen with a breakfast bar, granite countertops, custom cabinetry, and high-end appliances.

The third floor has two en-suite bedrooms and a den with coffered ceilings, a wood-burning fireplace, and access to a private terrace overlooking the carriage house.

Two king-sized bedroom suites with custom "study" areas are on the fourth floor.

A lavish primary suite spans the entire fifth floor. It features a south-facing sitting room that opens to a private terrace, a windowed dressing room, and a spa-inspired bathroom with a skylight, soaking tub, and a double vanity.

The sixth floor boasts a “skylit” fitness and wellness room along with a roof terrace “awaiting the next owner’s finishing touch.”

Schlisser said every prospective buyer she has shown the home to is interested in living there full-time.

“Carnegie Hill is a wonderful neighborhood,” she said. “Culturally and educationally, everything is there and the most frequented museums are there as well as some of the best private schools in Manhattan.”

The detached carriage house has cathedral ceilings, vertical-grain Douglas fir paneling, and a sleeping loft that could be used for guest accommodations or additional recreation space.

“I think the next buyer will be someone who is looking for space and proximity to schools,” Schlisser added. “The style is all new but very much a pre-war style. Everything has been done with incredible care. It’s really beautiful.”

#5445. Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, quickly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.)

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill said. “We went with commodity memory.”

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

“One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very quickly,” McCaskill said. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”

#5443. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5442. President Woodrow Wilson’s Historic Princeton Home Lists for $5.85 Million After a 7-Year Restoration

The home where Woodrow Wilson lived as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.

The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.

The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.

“Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” says listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty.

The estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing.

Blackwell says the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression.

The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors.

The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems.

The three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks.

The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with new matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds.

“The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell says.

Of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet.

Outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house.

The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away.

“This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a new home,” Blackwell says. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately.

Haas is not an outsider to Nvidia. He previously ran the company’s computing products business between 2006 and 2013, giving him direct experience with the company before its transformation into an AI powerhouse.

His subsequent run at Arm offers a glimpse of what he might bring to the role. Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for its fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. Its profit before tax climbed from $756 million to $960 million. The company has also moved beyond its traditional chip-design licensing business, introducing its own AGI CPU for AI data centers in March 2026.

Nvidia’s existing business gives him an enormous starting point. The company generated $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue in its latest results, with data center sales accounting for $107.6 billion. Revenue increased 103% from a year earlier.

Its next-generation Vera Rubin platform has also entered production and begun shipping. A new CEO would inherit an extraordinary growth engine, but also the responsibility of deciding how aggressively Nvidia should expand its influence across the AI industry.

If Haas brings his Arm strategy to Nvidia, we could see a push into integrated computing platforms, data center infrastructure and new AI applications. That could create another wave of investment across the technology sector.

Crypto could benefit if Haas turns Nvidia’s next chapter into another catalyst for AI infrastructure spending. The connection extends beyond tokens carrying artificial intelligence branding. Bitcoin and Ethereum have increasingly moved in tandem with technology stocks during periods when investors shift between risk assets.

A stronger Nvidia could help restore confidence in the AI investment cycle, especially if investors believe its leadership transition will not interrupt infrastructure spending.

Decentralized computing projects such as Render, Bittensor, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, and Akash could also benefit. These networks are trying to capture demand for GPU resources, distributed computing, and AI development.

More spending on AI infrastructure would create opportunities for decentralized alternatives. Developers need computing power, and centralized providers cannot always meet every requirement at the right price.

The bigger opportunity could come from investor appetite rather than immediate demand for crypto tokens. If Nvidia shares regain momentum under Rene Haas, technology investors could become more comfortable taking risks elsewhere. That would give crypto a potential source of buying interest.

Haas has already demonstrated what he can do with Arm. Taking over Nvidia would give him a considerably larger platform, with consequences extending well beyond semiconductor stocks.

#5440. Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”

Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.)

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller said. “We have to look for the data.”

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

“We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller said. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”

#5439. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5438. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

#5437. Housing Week Ahead: International Demand, Home Prices, and New-Home Sales

The coming week brings a number of key indicators and new research from the Realtor.com Economics team, despite the holiday schedule for Thanksgiving Day.

On Monday, new research from senior economist Hannah Jones shows that many Americans won't be traveling far to visit their parents for the holiday. That’s because a third of American adults under 35 years old still live in their parents’ home.

On Wednesday, senior economist Jiayi Xu has our third-quarter International Demand report, showing where home shoppers from different countries are looking at U.S. homes.

Also on Wednesday, coming out early due to the Thanksgiving holiday, senior economist Jake Krimmel will analyze our weekly housing data for clues on the latest housing market trends in real time.

For economic indicators being released next week, we’ll see the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Index on Tuesday, along with new-home sales and the Freddie Mac mortgage rate on Wednesday.

The Case-Shiller Index is expected to show national home price growth holding near 2% through September, after the national index rose 2.1% year over year through August. Annual gains have climbed since the spring, but slower median sales price growth and softer contract activity this summer suggest the pickup may be running out of steam.

New-home sales are likely to show another weak month in October, after falling 5.3% year over year in September. The existing-home segment saw softer pending home sales and home purchase closings last month as buyers are faced with affordability challenges due to high mortgage rates.

Despite more builders offering mortgage rate buydowns, the new-home segment is expected to be slowed down as well, as buyers’ budgets are stretched thin.

One thing I’ll be watching closely is the median new-home sales price, which has been lower than the median existing-home sales price for much of 2026, an intriguing result that mostly stems from where the new homes being sold are located.

The Freddie Mac average mortgage rate, which will come out on Wednesday instead of its usual Thursday, is likely to remain in the low-7% range, as the 10-Year Treasury yield remains elevated above 5% in advance of the expected rate hike by the Federal Reserve.

For full reports, the Market Clock, and raw housing data, visit realtor.com/research.

#5436. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5435. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5434. Robotics component maker coprod raises $6M to take on robotics ‘integration hell’

Robotics component maker coprod Inc. announced today that it has raised $6 million in new funding to reduce the time and costs associated with building new robotic platforms.

The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market. Founded in 2024, coprod offers an ecosystem of compatible hardware components for robotics and physical artificial intelligence applications.

It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.

At the core of coprod’s offering is the co:system, which combines the company’s modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane with one API in C++ and Python. The product family includes co:power, co:battery, co:sensor and co:motion, with each module able to be used as part of a complete system or integrated on its own.

Coprod is tackling the issue wherein most component suppliers support many protocols in the hope of catering to any integrator, which means their parts rarely work together out of the box. The result, according to coprod, is that building a system from mix-and-match components puts a heavy burden on the integrator. It requires two to three years of custom electronics and software work common before a system is reliable, in a phase known in the industry as “integration hell.”

The company claims that with its stack, the same work requires only a small team of roboticists, $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration and a few months of time.

“We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Loïc Delineau.

Coming into its new funding round, coprod’s components are already powering multiple robots in Switzerland, including the ETH Robotics Club’s XALUN, the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, which took its first steps in Zurich in recent weeks. The company is also establishing partnerships with robotics integrators and well-known labs to validate its first hardware prototypes before launching them on the market early next year.

The funding is also intended to support a new hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is expected to cut the company’s development cycles from two weeks to 24 hours. Testing at the site will be used to produce datasheets and digital twin models for each component, an effort aimed at narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world performance that arises in robotics development.

By the end of 2027, coprod plans to have its entire component line on the market, qualified and certified. Large-scale production is planned for both Shenzhen and Texas, with the company’s headquarters and research and development remaining in Switzerland.

Component supply has also emerged as a constraint for robot makers, particularly in humanoids. A McKinsey & Co. analysis published in April found that supply chain bottlenecks for humanoids are most likely to emerge around actuators and sensing and perception systems, the type of hardware coprod is developing.

Delineau formed coprod with Chief Technology Officer Vincent Nguyen and Chief Scientist Matthias Schuller (pictured), all graduates of the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. The three started out by building a bipedal robot demonstrator in a parent’s garage in the Swiss Alps to show what compatible components could do.

Founderful AG and Prototype Capital led the pre-seed round, with General Catalyst Group Management, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital and Venture Kick also participating. Angel investors in the round include Hugging Face Inc. co-founder Thomas Wolf, the Dassault family and Florent Perrichon. Venture Kick awarded coprod CHF 40,000 ($47,600) earlier this year.

Andreas Klinger, founder of Prototype, said coprod is fixing “the biggest problem in hardware.” It argues that robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware so they can focus on the parts of their products that create value for customers.
