#5389. Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data

Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data company, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.

A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.

The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The company said it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.

The company was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”

The company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.

“Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”

Aevius said the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the company’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.

The company is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.

On the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching issues faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.

“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.

#5387. NY Private-Listings Bill Becomes Law, Includes Opt-Out Option for Sellers

After passing both the state Assembly and Senate this past summer, the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act is now law after receiving New York Governor Kathy Hochul’s signature on Friday.

The law requires the “timely public advertising or marketing of listed residential properties on platforms accessible to the general public” but does provide an “opting-out” avenue for sellers who wish to market their listings privately, through a standardized state disclosure and process.

StreetEasy General Manager and Zillow Group (NYC) VP Caroline Burton applauds Hochul and describes the state of New York City housing, pointing to scarcity issues keeping affordability out of reach.

“This is a win for all buyers, sellers, and the agents who serve them,” she states. “When homes are kept out of public view, New Yorkers lose out, especially in a market where homes for sale are already scarce. Our research shows that the overwhelming majority of NYC buyers want to see all of the options available to them, and many NYC sellers who listed privately ended up regretting it.”

A Compass spokesperson commended Hochul for signing the bill into law, commenting the new law “preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes.”

The New York State Association of Realtors® (NYSAR) praises the governor and stated that the legislation “promotes greater transparency and consumer protection in the real estate marketplace by addressing the use of private listing networks.”

“This new law helps ensure that property owners are fully informed of the potential consequences of limiting the public marketing of their properties, including the possibility of reduced exposure to prospective buyers or tenants,” the association states. “Importantly, the legislation strikes an appropriate balance between promoting transparency and protecting consumer choice by preserving the ability of property owners to determine how their properties are marketed.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

During the law’s drafting and path through each of the legislative bodies, Mike Kelly— NYSAR VP and chief lobbyist of Government Affairs—expressed the association’s support for the bill to RISMedia and had high hopes for the changes to come for the state’s housing market.

“The legislation starts with the premise that the real estate licensee, the professional representative, seller or lessor is required to widely market their property,” he said. “But in cases where the lessor seller wants to enter into a private listing network or limited marketing, they can do so, but they can only do so by acknowledging and signing a state required disclosure form.”

The act was originally introduced by Assemblywoman Michaelle C. Solages (D-NY)— who represents New York’s District 22 in the state legislature—and she described “transparency” as her main intention for the bill to RISMedia.

“It’s always been my goal as a state legislator to ensure that folks have access to the housing market,” she said. “So whether it’s finding discrimination, building more supply, or making sure that we have transparency with private listing networks, this is a goal to ensure that we are giving people access to the housing market. The legislation really is about transparency, fairness and access.”

Anthony Domathoti, treasurer and incoming president-elect 2027 for the NYSAR, states the law is a “real win for consumer and for transparency” in the market.

“In my 27 years as a broker, I’ve seen how much exposure matters when you sell or rent a property,” he added. “When an owner keeps a listing off the open market, fewer buyers and tenants ever see it. This law makes owners understand that tradeoff before they decide. The Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act’s signing is just the latest in changes to private listing networks. What I like most is that it doesn’t take the decision away from them. Owners still choose how their property gets marketed. They just make that choice with full information.”

In May of this year, Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont also signed a similar bill into law to reform real estate in the Constitution State. Like New York’s version, the Connecticut law does not outright ban the use of private listing networks, rather it mandates that if a listing is added to such a network, it must also be marketed on a public platform.

Connecticut’s law also includes an opt-out option from public marketing, ensuring that sellers are informed and educated prior to making their decision on whether to publicly or privately market their properties.

“Finding a home in the most challenging market shouldn’t depend on privilege, who you know, or who you work with,” Burton added. “In one of the biggest decisions in a person’s life, New Yorkers deserve an open and transparent marketplace so they can make an informed choice.”

Editor’s Note: This story was updated 3:17 p.m. Eastern Time with a comment from a Compass, Inc. spokesperson.

#5386. Trump Memecoin Dinner? Investors Wait for a Miracle

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Donald Trump is preparing another exclusive dinner for his biggest memecoin supporters, but the invitation is becoming cheaper as his token continues to collapse. The TRUMP token is down almost 99% from its peak, and this time, the presidential dinner contest closed with just 130 participating wallets holding $8.6 million, despite organizers offering 185 places.

The dinner will welcome the largest holders at Trump’s Virginia golf club on November 22. The top 29 receive an additional VIP reception, while other token holders are left watching from outside.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 President Trump to host exclusive dinner for top holders of his $TRUMP crypto memecoin on Sunday.

Just last year, wealthy buyers competed for access to Trump with millions of dollars in token purchases. This time, more than 5,000 eligible holders reportedly declined to register, while one successful entrant qualified with just $518 in purchases.

The upcoming celebration offers little reason to celebrate, as holders watched millions disappear from their holdings during the competition.

The shrinking competition exposes a problem that another presidential appearance cannot easily fix. TRUMP first memecoin dinner generated considerable excitement around the token, attracting buyers who wanted proximity to Trump and exposure to his political brand. That enthusiasm has since faded alongside the price.

Trump’s family has reportedly earned at least $635 million from the memecoin through April, according to financial disclosures and reported estimates. Meanwhile, outside investors have suffered substantial losses across several Trump-linked crypto ventures.

So, what happens to everyone who bought the token but never gets an invitation?

There is no comparable VIP experience for ordinary investors who purchased during the rally and are now sitting on losses. They cannot simply exchange their depreciated holdings for access to the president.

The frustration extends beyond TRUMP. MELANIA memecoin has also suffered a dramatic collapse from its launch-era highs, weakening confidence in the wider family-branded token ecosystem. Investors who bought into the political momentum now face a difficult question about what sustains demand once the initial excitement disappears.

World Liberty Financial is another broken painting. Its WLFI governance token has fallen towards $0.045, close to its all-time low of $0.0437. A substantial retreat from its September 2025 peak near $0.33.

Its USD1 stablecoin has also seen its market cap retreat from $4.4 billion in early October to around $2.9 billion today.

These are different products with different purposes, but their declining market valuations put pressure on the Trump-linked crypto narrative.

From bad comes to worse. Justin Sun, Tron founder, was among the most prominent early supporters of World Liberty Financial and attended Trump’s inaugural memecoin dinner. His WLFI holdings were frozen by the project, prompting him to file a lawsuit against the company just a few months ago.

The concern is no longer simply if all of Trump’s linked tokens can recover.

The market environment is hardly helping speculative assets. Iran war continues to disrupt commercial shipping and keep geopolitical risk in financial markets. Renewed attacks around Riyadh and reported tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz pushed oil prices higher on Friday.

Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was struck in a Houthi attack in the latest blow in the Iran-backed Yemeni group's war with the kingdom https://t.co/5JdXw4PKS3 pic.twitter.com/xlQvZIv7ZX

Brent crude hovers at $92, while US West Texas Intermediate reached $83. Both benchmarks were nevertheless heading for another weekly decline as expectations of a global supply surplus offset renewed geopolitical concerns.

For us, the problem extends beyond oil prices. Energy disruptions can feed inflation concerns, complicate interest-rate expectations and undermine appetite for riskier investments.

Memecoins have little protection when speculative demand disappears. The political branding behind the TRUMP memecoin cannot guarantee buyers will return after the dinner, especially when holders are dealing with substantial losses.

Trump can still host another dinner and welcome his biggest memecoin supporters, but the event cannot answer the question facing thousands of ordinary holders.

#5385. Why an Uninsulated Garage Can Wreak Havoc on Your Home This Winter

An uninsulated garage might seem like no big deal, but come the winter months, it can do more harm than good.

In fact, when a garage lacks proper insulation during the colder months, frozen pipes, heat loss, and damaged items are bound to arise.

Fortunately, insulation solutions and preventive measures can help you avoid these issues while protecting your garage, your car, and your home.

An uninsulated garage in the winter months can cause a chain reaction of issues to the home itself. One of the most common risks is frozen pipes.

“When the plumbing or water lines located in the garage get exposed to below-freezing temps, they may freeze and cause water damage,” explains Chris Boyle, in-house repair tech at Parts Town Home and Fix.com in Nova Scotia.

Additionally, improperly insulated garages can prompt heat loss throughout the entire home.

“Many poorly insulated garages share foundations with homes. As a result, cold air may circulate through the living spaces and force families to turn up their heating systems,” says Boyle.

Not only does this put a strain on HVAC systems, it can also drive up monthly heating bills.

Plus, poor insulation may damage items stored in the garage, particularly car batteries, which can lose charge or fail completely.

So, how do you know for sure whether your garage is insulated?

On a cold day, compare the temperature inside your garage to the outside.

If your garage feels as cold as the outdoors, or if the rooms adjacent to it are always noticeably colder in the winter, there’s a good chance it’s not insulated.

“You can also inspect the walls and ceiling for visible insulation. On the garage door, thin or hollow panels usually indicate a lack of insulation, while thicker panels often mean insulating material is present,” explains Paul Sharpe, owner at Surfside Garage Doors in Toms River, NJ.

Once you determine you have an uninsulated garage, here are several tips to keep on your radar.

For a faster, practical insulation solution, seal any of the bottom gaps under your garage door with rubber weatherstripping.

“If your budget and resources allow, however, the most effective way to retain heat in your garage is to insulate all the walls with fiberglass insulation,” says Chris Hunter, director of customer relations at ServiceTitan in Glendale, CA.

Regardless of your choice, these solutions will help decrease your energy bill and create a more comfortable environment.

Since the garage door is the largest opening in your home, investing in an insulated garage door may be worthwhile. Entry-level insulated doors typically provide an R-value between 6 and 9, while higher-end models can reach R-values of around 20.

“The higher the R-value, the higher the insulation capabilities and less heat loss that will occur,” explains Sharpe.

You don’t have to expose your valuables to the risks of an uninsulated garage.

“To avoid damaging your items in the garage during winter, you may either elevate them or bring them inside your insulated home,” says Tamer Sayed, licensed HVAC technician and the owner-operator of Tamas Mechanical in Mississauga, Ontario.

Before the winter begins (or even after, if you missed the boat), consult an HVAC professional for an insulation evaluation. The pro can determine whether your garage is properly safeguarded for the season and recommend the best next steps.

#5384. AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

Amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.

Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a new family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.

AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

After introducing Strands Harness, which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS said decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.

With Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.

The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.

So far, AWS has used the Strands Decider v2 agents only internally, but it has seen impressive results. For instance, its engineers were able to replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on the company’s largest internal ticketing system, and in the process they were able to reduce its labelling costs by 98%.

They also cut ticket response times by 78%. But that’s not all they can do – in its experiments, AWS said, the new decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models when a more computationally intensive frontier model might be overkill.

The Strands Decider v2 models are available to everyone now under an Apache 2.0 license and can be found on Hugging Face and also the Strands Decider repository on AWS.

Strands Decider is all about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. Meanwhile, Box CLI is all about securing them.

In a second blog post, AWS explained that many developers have taken to running their coding agents in what’s known as “YOLO mode.” That’s where they disable permission and configuration prompts so that those agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools as they see fit in order to complete a task. It’s named after the slang phrase “you only live once.”

Agents running in YOLO mode execute much faster, but they do so at the sacrifice of human oversight. And that’s dangerous. An agent without any restrictions can accidentally delete files it really shouldn’t or leak sensitive keys, or it can be manipulated through a malicious prompt to do something else that’s extremely damaging.

AWS’ solution to this is Strands Box, which is an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action. It launched last month, and with today’s update, it’s getting a new Box CLI that adds support for coding agents including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and the company’s very own Kiro CLI.

The idea is that developers can wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox to prevent any accidents from occurring. Within the sandbox, the agents will be able to work without restrictions, meaning they won’t have to keep pausing to ask a human developer for permission to do something important.

Instead, the developer simply applies security policies to safeguard the agent’s actions. These policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access, AWS explained.

The agent’s credentials live outside the sandbox, with application programming interface keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment. That way, the agent itself never has access to those sensitive keys.

AWS said developers also have the flexibility to switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access.

Like the new decider models, Box CLI in Strands Box is being launched today. It’s a big step forward for autonomous agents, ensuring they can work without constant interruptions while remaining on a very short leash.

#5383. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5382. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5380. Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees

Buying a home comes with enough expenses already. Between inspections, title insurance, closing costs, and a stack of paperwork that seems to grow every day, it's easy to lose track of what you're paying for.

But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills?

It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer.

Employer-sponsored legal plans, offered through companies such as LegalShield, MetLife and ARAG, can provide access to attorneys for a modest monthly fee.

A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Depending on the plan, some or all of that may be covered.

Jago Gavin, a LegalShield representative who works with employer groups, tells Realtor.com® that the real value is having someone to consult before signing something you might not fully understand.

"The law is not logical; it's legal," Gavin says.

That's relevant when buying a house, where an unfamiliar contract provision can have expensive consequences.

Gavin recalls a LegalShield member whose attorney spotted a potentially unfavorable mediation clause in real estate paperwork and recommended changing it before the buyer signed.

The potential savings can run from hundreds to thousands of dollars. But there's a catch: Not all legal plans offer the same services, and buyers need to know what they're getting before signing up.

Group legal plans work much like other voluntary workplace benefits. Employees pay a monthly premium, usually through payroll deductions, in exchange for access to specified legal services.

The price can be surprisingly affordable.

In a review of publicly available employee benefits documents, Realtor.com found a plan offered to employees of financial technology company Fiserv through MetLife for $15.50 monthly. LegalShield's published employer plans generally cost about $19 to $25 a month, depending on the coverage and employer.

That's roughly $186 to $300 annually, potentially less than the cost of a single consultation with a private attorney.

The plans typically provide access to participating law firms that handle matters ranging from contract reviews and consumer disputes to estate planning. Some cover specific services in full, while others offer discounted rates for legal work outside the plan.

ContractsCounsel, an online marketplace connecting clients with attorneys, reports that lawyers on its platform charged an average flat fee of $620 to review a real estate purchase agreement, based on completed projects.

Compare that with LegalShield's published Choice plan, which costs $21.95 monthly, or $263.40 over a year.

If an employee uses the plan for comparable document-review work without additional charges, the potential savings could be about $350.

But reviewing a contract and representing someone throughout a real estate transaction are two very different services.

LegalShield's published employer-plan documents include certain residential mortgage-document reviews but specifically exclude an attorney's attendance at closing. Documents must also be provided at least five business days before the scheduled closing.

An ARAG legal plan available to University of California employees, for example, pays participating attorneys for covered services that include reviewing and preparing home purchase documents and attending a closing. California doesn't generally require attorneys at residential closings, but the benefit illustrates how coverage can extend beyond reviewing paperwork.

The MetLife plan offered to Fiserv employees also lists home purchases and sales among its covered services. MetLife plan descriptions published by several other employers go further, listing deeds, boundary and title disputes, and property tax assessments—handy if a new owner wants to challenge a tax bill after the purchase. Employees should still check precisely what their particular plan includes.

And even comprehensive coverage won't eliminate ordinary closing expenses. Buyers are generally still responsible for title insurance, recording fees, taxes and other third-party charges.

New York real estate attorney Adam Leitman Bailey sees the obvious appeal: lower costs. But he questions whether attorneys with busy, established practices have much incentive to participate in programs requiring them to accept reduced fees.

For a relatively straightforward transaction, that might not matter much, he says. But complicated purchases can be another story.

"When something goes wrong, and this is the biggest investment of your lifetime, you'd better believe that you should be hiring the best attorney you can," Bailey tells Realtor.com.

That doesn't mean attorneys participating in group plans are necessarily less qualified. It does mean buyers should ask about their experience, particularly if a transaction involves title disputes, unusual contract provisions, or other complications.

Gavin acknowledges that LegalShield sometimes encounters coverage gaps in rural areas, where the nearest participating firm may be hours away.

Some plans offer referrals, discounted services, or reimbursement for using attorneys outside their networks, but those benefits vary.

Before relying on a workplace plan to handle a purchase, buyers should make sure an appropriate attorney is available and that the services they need are actually covered.

Buying a home is also a good time to think about what happens to the property in the future.

Many employer legal plans include estate planning services such as preparing wills and powers of attorney.

Some also help with living trusts, whether revocable, which can be changed later, or irrevocable, which generally can't. Either can help manage and transfer assets, and property properly placed in a trust can typically avoid probate.

These services can be expensive on their own. A March 2026 study by LegalTemplates, drawing on pricing from 909 law firms nationwide, found a median price of $625 for a standalone will and $2,475 for a revocable living trust.

By comparison, some employer legal plans include those services in the annual premium, potentially saving homeowners considerably more than they pay for coverage.

Becci Powers-Johnson, an eight-year LegalShield retail customer who became an independent associate selling its services in August 2026, says she and her fiancé have used the program several times to update their wills, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives.

"It was more than just the forms; it was the consultations that were included with it," she says. LegalShield offers unlimited consultations.

Of course, not every homeowner needs a trust, and some plans charge extra for preparing one or transferring property into it. The appropriate documents depend on individual circumstances and state law.

If you're thinking about buying a home in the coming year, take another look at your workplace benefits before open enrollment ends.

Start with your state's rules. Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Massachusetts, South Carolina, and West Virginia are among the states that require or customarily expect an attorney's involvement at closing, according to the National Notary Association, and in places like New York, it's standard practice. Elsewhere, a title or escrow company usually handles the closing, so full closing representation may matter more in some states than others.

Then check the plan itself. Does it cover purchase agreements, title and deed work, mortgage paperwork, or full closing representation? Is there an attorney near you who handles real estate transactions? And what happens if you need more complicated legal work?

Timing matters, too. You can typically sign up only when you're hired or during open enrollment, and many plans expect you to stay in for the full plan year.

George Washington University, for one, doesn't let employees cancel until the open enrollment after 12 months in the plan. Others allow cancellation at any time but make you wait until the next enrollment period to rejoin. And matters already underway may not qualify for coverage.

Even a relatively inexpensive plan isn't necessarily worthwhile if you never use it. But for someone preparing to purchase a home, the right benefit could pay for itself with just one covered legal service.

#5379. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5378. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5377. CrowdStrike’s Zscaler deal is a $44B vote for platformization and a long-term threat to Palo Alto Networks

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.

This has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product. The reality is that choosing best-of-breed everywhere has never led to best-in-class threat protection.

Palo Alto Networks Inc. has long articulated the value of security platformization. To be precise, Fortinet Inc. was the first vendor to advance the concept of a security platform, but no security provider has pushed the industry as hard as Palo Alto. Chief Executice Nikesh Arora has been vocal about platforms as the only way to truly protect the entire attack surface.

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s agreement to acquire Zscaler Inc. for $43.9 billion strongly supports the thesis. SiliconANGLE has been covering the deal, so I won’t rehash the details. In short, the leader in endpoint security is buying the leader in cloud-delivered zero-trust access. The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, and the deal is expected to close between August 2027 and January 2028.

Over the long term, the combination poses a real threat to Palo Alto. In the short term, it is a strong co-sell opportunity for CrowdStrike and Zscaler, with significant integration work between the two.

Arora has long argued that customers want fewer vendors and integrated platforms. Getting there can be challenging, as security teams often operate with an “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” mentality. The mere thought of replacing a working product is enough to keep even the most seasoned security pros up at night. In February 2024, when he cut guidance to fund the platform push, Palo Alto’s stock fell 28% in a day. Since then, the stock has recovered nicely, validating his strategy, and its rival has now raised $44 billion to head down its own platform journey.

In some ways, CrowdStrike and Zscaler were the strongest argument against platformization, though one could argue that each was its own smaller “platform,” depending on how you define it. Each led its category, and the two were close partners, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 product integrations. If best-of-breed products, tied together by integrations, could work anywhere, it was here. The two companies are now taking it a step further. “When you integrate as partners, there’s only so much you can do,” Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry said on the analyst call.

The “why now?” question is worth asking, as the coming together of these two companies has been rumored for some time. The answer is that agentic AI creates new challenges and risks that are difficult to address through a partnership. An AI agent runs on a device and then crosses the network to access models, tools, and data, operating at machine speed around the clock. A vendor that sees only the device or only the network sees only half of what the agent does. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said adversaries are “exploiting the seams and the gaps between companies’ integrations.”

I agree. Every seam between products is a place for an attacker to hide, and AI-driven attacks exploit those seams faster than security teams can close them. But a platform is more than one vendor and one contract. It means one dataset, one agent, and one policy engine, so a detection on a laptop triggers enforcement across the network without a person in the middle. If that’s the standard, CrowdStrike, while it currently describes itself as a platform, is not today.

With Zscaler, CrowdStrike is more than just a product to fill a gap. Zscaler is a best-in-class Secure Access Service Edge stack that protects half of the Fortune 500 and runs what it calls the world’s largest inline security cloud.

It is also built for resilience, which matters more than ever. Last week, I wrote about six major outages over six days at organizations ranging from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration. Zscaler sits between every user and every application, so if it fails, the business stops. That has forced the company to engineer for failure.

Its Business Continuity Cloud provides each customer with a dedicated backup environment in third-party data centers, on separate networks and DNS, with software updates deliberately staggered so a bad release can’t affect both simultaneously. “No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry told me in a previous conversation.

Of all companies, CrowdStrike should value that. In July 2024, a faulty Falcon update affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices. The standard objection to platformization is concentration risk, and it intensifies when a single vendor controls both the endpoint agent and the path to every application. Zscaler’s continuity design is the best answer to that objection I’ve seen, and CrowdStrike should extend it across Falcon.

The near-term value is commercial. CrowdStrike says about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet buy from it. Channel partners already sell both companies, and the two sales teams already work deals together.

After the close, Zscaler will transition to Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike’s licensing model. “A Zscaler customer can add Falcon. A Falcon customer can add Zscaler. One contract, one platform,” Kurtz said. CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

This target seems bullish but achievable, as it requires no code integration — only sales execution, which both companies are good at.

Today, the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds with different release schedules. Kurtz promised that it will collapse into one. “The brand promise, single agent, that’s not going to change,” he said. CrowdStrike’s next-generation sensor can already inspect and proxy network traffic, he added, which should make the job easier.

Kurtz was also candid about the effort: “Yes, there’s hard work to be done. There always is in an acquisition.” CrowdStrike gave no timeline. The engineering teams can’t combine until the deal closes, which is at least eight months away. CrowdStrike’s largest prior acquisition cost less than $1 billion. Folding Zscaler’s global security cloud into Falcon is far harder than anything it has attempted. Until that work is done, the platform exists on slides.

That gap gives Palo Alto time to further its own platform. It closed its CyberArk acquisition in February, renamed the business Idira, and is already cross-selling it to its existing customers.

The long term looks different. If CrowdStrike delivers a single agent and a single dataset, Palo Alto will face something it hasn’t had: a rival of similar scale with the leading endpoint product and the leading zero-trust cloud on one platform. Palo Alto is most exposed in SASE, where its Prisma SASE business has been chasing Zscaler.

CrowdStrike plus Zscaler make a formidable platform, but it still lacks a firewall. Zscaler is a cloud proxy, and many enterprises that use it still run firewalls in their data centers, campuses, and clouds. That is Palo Alto’s core area of strength.

Looking ahead, that should open the door to another acquisition. Check Point is the obvious choice, as it will struggle over the long term as a firewall pure-play in a market shifting to platforms, and it would give CrowdStrike a large installed base. If CrowdStrike wants a broader networking portfolio, Fortinet is the bigger swing, with switching, wireless and software-defined wide-area network alongside its firewalls. The two already partner on endpoint and firewall protection.

Either deal would add more integration work to Zscaler, so I wouldn’t expect either to happen soon. But a company that wants to displace Palo Alto can’t leave the firewall to someone else forever. I understand zero trust can replace a number of firewalls, particularly in branch offices, but firewalls are here to stay for the foreseeable future.

The deal also puts smaller security vendors in play. Netskope and Cato Networks are both independent SASE vendors competing against a bundle, and Oppenheimer has already named Netskope an attractive target.

Fortinet is an obvious acquirer, but the buyer pool extends beyond security companies. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., following its acquisition of Juniper Networks Inc., is embedding security across its network and may seek to bolster that portfolio. Dell Technologies Inc. lags in security, with a portfolio centered on data protection and resilience, and could benefit from an acquisition to close the gap.

Nothing changes today, and customers shouldn’t pause their projects. I’d use the waiting period to prepare in advance.

Buy what is integrated. Ask for the integration roadmap with dates for the single agent, the shared data set and unified policy. Until those ship, evaluate CrowdStrike and Zscaler as two products.

Use leverage. Palo Alto is trying to pry Zscaler accounts loose, and CrowdStrike and Zscaler want commitments before the close. As Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research told CSO, “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second.” Negotiate price caps for renewals now.

Get interoperability in writing. When asked about lock-in, Kurtz said, “We have and will continue to work well with all of the other technologies and ecosystem.” If you run Zscaler with another endpoint product or Falcon with another access provider, include that promise in your contract.

Make resilience a requirement. Ask CrowdStrike to commit to maintaining Zscaler’s Business Continuity Cloud and its staggered updates, and to apply the same discipline to a combined agent.

This deal settles the argument over platformization. Who wins is still unclear. CrowdStrike has to do the integration work, and Palo Alto has the better part of a year to persuade customers not to wait. The great news for customers is that big moves like this create a wave of innovation. AI is changing security faster than ever before, and a CrowdStrike-vs.-Palo Alto battle is good for everyone.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5376. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5375. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul Signs New Private Listings Bill

New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent.

Late last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listing Act. The language of the bill requires that real estate listings be marketed in "at least one other publication, platform or website that does not require payment" or for the consumer to work with the brokerage for access.

This follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June. The New York State Association of Realtors® strongly supports the bill.

This becomes the latest crackdown on private listings, where a real estate agent markets a property to a limited list of buyers before making it public.

Fair housing advocates say private listings raise discrimination concerns. One study from Bright MLS found private listings take longer to sell and don't guarantee more money.

The listing must be accessible to the general public, "without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise or select group of licenses." Also, there can't be restrictions on some or all of the details in the listing, according to the language of the bill.

The bill doesn't require a seller or lister to hold open houses or public showings if it violates any state or federal laws related to health and safety. And sellers can opt out, by signing a form that explicitly warns them that the listing will have limited visibility and possible impact on the price they get.

New York can punish violators with a fine of up to $5,000 and suspension or revocation of  their real estate license.

Earlier this year, the state saw its inventory of homes for sale fall to a 30-year low.

Washington and Connecticut have passed similar laws this year. Each has generally similar language in their bills, which also allow for opt-outs. A study from Zillow found the sales price of private listings was 1.3% less than comparable sales on the multiple listing service, costing the seller an average of $4,230 per sale. (Realtor.com® recently struck an agreement with Zillow to show preview listings from brokers who participate in Zillow’s preview program, in an effort to boost market transparency.)

Compass Inc., the real estate brokerage giant which has defended its use of private listings, said its recently unveiled See It First listings strategy complies with the law. It launched that program in September, which gives early access to homes that will soon be listed on the public market. Users don't need to work with a Compass agent to use it.

"New York’s new law preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes, including the ability to use a See It First strategy to test pricing and gauge demand," a Compass spokesperson said. "See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market."

New York has long struggled with housing affordability. The Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card gave the Empire State an F, the lowest rating possible. Hochul has emphasized affordability concerns and made a deregulation push to make home construction easier.

“My administration is focused on making New York more affordable and liveable for every New Yorker regardless of age or income, and housing is central to that goal,” Hochul said last week.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.
