#5341. Human review remains paramount for AI mortgage underwriting

Leaders at Incenter Diligence Solutions and SitusAMC say AI can index, extract and flag inconsistencies across mortgage documents, improving review speed. They caution that blank fields, unusual scenarios and model behavior require human validation, plus ongoing testing and QC.  AI Summary

Artificial intelligence is helping mortgage lenders and due-diligence firms review loan files and extract borrower information, but integrating AI into underwriting processes isn’t a one-and-done experience. The technology still needs human oversight, experts say, especially when loans involve unusual circumstances or require judgment beyond standard guidelines.

At Incenter Diligence Solutions, AI has accelerated document indexing and data extraction, according to president Pamela Hamrick. Technology can now sort and categorize thousands of pages of loan documents in minutes, replacing a process that once required employees to manually separate and label files.

Hamrick said that while AI can extract information from standardized mortgage documents like loan estimates and closing disclosures, borrower-provided records — including pay stubs and bank statements. — are harder to process because their formats vary.

AI, however, can identify inconsistencies across documents and summarize them for underwriters to investigate.

“The technology is identifying the questions, and the inconsistencies and the anomalies, between all of this documentation, and summarizing that for an underwriter or a reviewer … to dig deeper and make a decision about whether or not what the AI has identified is a real risk — or if it’s a minimal risk or maybe it’s no risk at all because of the particular scenario,” Hamrick said in an interview with HousingWire.

Julia Curran, senior managing director of residential AI products at SitusAMC, said the company uses AI to re-underwrite closed loans in the secondary market, checking regulatory and underwriting guidelines as well as data accuracy before loans are reviewed for securitization.

According to Curran, SitusAMC builds AI agents around processes established by human subject matter experts and tests their results against loans previously reviewed by people. She said the company runs repeated tests until the system reaches at least 95% accuracy.

But the technology still needs the human touch. Curran said the system sends blank or inconsistent fields to human reviewers, and final credit decisions require judgments that cannot be reduced to individual data points.

“A final credit decision shouldn’t be made by the machine because there’s other things to consider besides the specific data points,” Curran said.

Hamrick added: “Companies that fully rely on AI are potentially going to have misses in some other areas where a human might have been able to make a different decision.”

Curran also warned about the AI model supplying information not supported or provided by the documents submitted. She described a case in which a model supplied a solar panel number that was not included in a particular loan file. The answer was correct, but the system had apparently drawn on information from other files.

“Even though it’s right, I don’t want that answer,” Curran said. “I want to stay within the four walls of this file.”

The executives said lenders should test AI against established human processes before relying on it for underwriting.

Hamrick recommended introducing the technology in one part of the workflow at a time, comparing its results with human reviews before expanding its use. She also said lenders should prepare employees for changes by retraining them for tasks that require more human intervention.

“The best thing that we can do as leaders is look where the technology can ultimately take over, and then take the folks that are doing those roles and train them to be better at the things that require more human intervention,” she said.

Curran said quality control requires testing models across different loan types and scenarios. SitusAMC maintains a test bank of hundreds of previously reviewed loans, including purchases, refinances, adjustable-rate mortgages and loans with rate buydowns. When a model changes, the company runs its prompts against the test bank to check whether results remain consistent.

These tests add costs that lenders may overlook. Curran said companies should ask AI vendors how their systems were developed, whether subject matter experts helped establish the processes and whether ongoing regression testing is in place.

“You want the same answer every time,” Curran said. “The process of taking a non-deterministic process and making it deterministic takes a lot of time and effort.”

#5339. Mortgage headlines aren’t as big a concern as your cost per closing

The piece frames 2027 as a consolidation year, with equity strong but deal counts pressured by affordability. It urges teams to track cost per closing by source, stress-test a 20% volume drop, and shift toward sellers, sphere and longer follow-up.  AI Summary

If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027.

I understand why it spread. Freddie Mac had the 30-year fixed at 7.28% on Oct. 1, up from 6.01% in February and the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. If everything moves the wrong way at once, 9% could sound possible.

The Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments. It is likely causing some anxiety for many agents.

It helps to look at what it would actually take. Cotality’s chief economist, Selma Hepp, raised 9% on CNBC as a worst case, not a forecast. HousingWire’s Logan Mohtashami laid out the math: the 10-year would have to push past 6%, and mortgage spreads would have to widen well beyond the roughly 2% they sit at today. That requires a hot economy, oil prices that stay high and a Fed that keeps hiking past what markets expect, all lasting well into next year. September’s jobs report showed 29,000 new jobs, which already works against the hot-economy part.

So I wouldn’t plan around 9%. I also wouldn’t plan around rates falling back to 6% anytime soon. The Fed’s own projections show no cuts in 2027, and the Mortgage Bankers Association expects rates to stay close to where they are.

A crash needs forced sellers, and we don’t have many. Homeowners with a mortgage carry an average loan-to-value of about 44%, and only around 2% are underwater, according to Cotality. That isn’t 2008.

What we do have is fewer deals. In early October, pending sales were about 10% less than the year before, and purchase applications were down 14%. Those applications turn into closings 30 to 90 days later, so a lot of teams have been looking at a softer first quarter. At today’s rate, the payment that covered a $400,000 loan in February covers about $357,000 now. Same buyer, same budget, about 11% less loan.

Prices mostly hold, and the deal count shrinks. I think of 2027 as a consolidation year rather than a crash year.

In August, I wrote here that cost-per-lead is the wrong number to run a team on, and that cost-per-closed deal is the one that tells you the truth. A slow year is when that stops being a philosophy and turns into a real potential problem.

Most of what a team spends to generate business is fixed. The ad campaign, vendor contracts, the ISA hours and the coaching all get billed whether deals close or not. When conversion falls, none of those invoices get smaller.

Say a team spends $6,000 a month on lead generation and closes 12 deals a quarter from it. That’s $1,500 per closing. Then buyer conversion slips, and the same spend produces nine closings. Now each closing costs $2,000. Nothing on the invoice changed, and every deal got a third more expensive.

That’s the exposure I’d worry about: a cost structure built for a 6.5% market, running in a 7.5% one.

The gap between a team that knows its number and one that doesn’t gets much wider when volume drops.

You can’t control the 10-year Treasury. These are the things you can control though:

Find your cost per closing by source. Add up everything you spend on each lead source, including ad spend, platform and referral fees, ISA time and software, and divide it by the closed transactions that source produced over the last 12 months. Use closings, not appointments or signed agreements. Most team leads I talk to have never broken this out by source, and the answer usually surprises them.

Stress-test it at a lower deal count. Run the same numbers assuming 20% fewer closings. Any source that ends up costing more per closing than your net is one to fix or cut now, while you still have room to choose.

Shift your mix toward sellers and your sphere. Buyers are the first to stall when rates jump. Sellers still have to move for new jobs, divorces, estates, and growing families, whatever the rate happens to be, and your past clients are sitting on real equity. If most of your pipeline is buyer leads, 2027 will hurt more than it should.

Lengthen your nurture instead of cutting it. The buyer who is priced out at 7.5% may be ready at 6.75%. If your follow-up ends at 90 days, someone else gets that deal if rates turn, and you end up paying for the same lead twice.

Give your agents training so they can handle these clients. Don’t promise rates will fall. Understand the concern first, then help the buyer evaluate actual numbers without treating a forecast as a fact.

2023 had the fewest existing-home sales since 1995. The teams I watched hold up through it weren’t the ones that guessed right about rates. They were the ones that knew what each closing cost them and kept moving money toward what was working.

There will be another very scary hot topic after this one, and another after that. The best hedge against all of them is the same: know your cost per closing, and build a pipeline that doesn’t depend on buyers feeling good about rates.

Robyn Thompson DeSantos is the founder and CEO of Ascension Group, a business solutions and management company for real estate team leaders and brokers.

#5338. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

#5336. FHA’s reverse mortgage book faces headwinds from home prices, fewer payoffs

FHA’s 2026 Annual Report to Congress shows its HECM reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile part of the Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund. The HECM standalone capital ratio fell from 24.06% to 5.43% in one year, driven by slower home price growth, fewer loan payoffs and heavy assignment claim spending, though it stayed above the 2% statutory minimum.   AI Summary

The Federal Housing Administration’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress says the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year.

The report, released Nov. 16, found that the MMI Fund’s overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept. 30, moving from 11.47% last year to 10.29% this year. The current figure, however, is roughly five times higher than fund’s statutory minimum requirement of 2%.

Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026. The FHA attributed this decline mainly to macroeconomic dynamics and program-specific cash flows.

The reverse mortgage portfolio, which accounts for less than 4% of the fund’s insurance in force, is “much more sensitive to home prices,” the report explained. Slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts have increased projected losses for the HECM program. In addition, loan payoffs — which represent more favorable recovery outcomes than other disposition methods like foreclosures — have become less common and have pushed losses higher.

The agency also noted that the HECM program “spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.” These claims, which are generated when FHA acquires loans that hit the 98% maximum claim amount threshold, are a known driver of volatility in the HECM book. They remain a key cost to monitor for reverse mortgage issuers and servicers.

While the federally insured reverse mortgage portfolio is still in the black, the takeaway from the report is that its capital support can change rapidly due to shifts in home price appreciation, payoff behaviors and the frequency of assignment claims. These factors drive FHA policy decisions, as well as Ginnie Mae execution in the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) market.

The report illustrates that FHA-insured options remain central to the wider reverse mortgage market, even as volumes edge lower. In FY 2026, FHA insured 24,162 HECMs representing a maximum claim amount (MCA) of $12.81 billion.

Endorsements were down about 14% from the 28,149 HECMs endorsed in FY 2025. MCA volume also fell from about $15.5 billion in 2025 to roughly $13.5 billion in 2026.

But even with that pullback, the HECM program “remains a large part of the market,” according to the report. Historic data reinforces the sector’s structural shift. HECM endorsements peaked above 110,000 in 2009 with roughly $30.5 billion in MCA. Volumes have trended lower for more than a decade, with visible rebounds in 2020–2022 during a period of low interest rates and high home price growth. But higher rates and slower price growth since 2023 have softened demand.

To fill the gap, lenders are focusing on proprietary reverse mortgages through their retail, wholesale and correspondent channels. The wider availability of these products has propelled a shift in market share as private-label loans accounted for more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September, according to New View Advisors.

“I think that product diversity is great because we’re able to serve more clients that the FHA product wouldn’t handle,” Jesse Allen, president of 55+ lending at Rate, told HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD) at this month’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo.

He said these may be “mass affluent clients who have home values of $2 million or $3 million, and they really want to tap their equity without the debt service to achieve their goals,” but they can also be clients who don’t fit the HECM qualification requirements and are using reverse mortgage proceeds to consolidate debt.

“This is another regulatory guideline NRMLA has advocated for. ‘Hey, we’re paying off consumer debts. Let’s not count that toward the the qualification process.’ Proprietary allows us to do that and HECM does not,” Allen said.

FHA’s FY 2026 report includes a dedicated HECM chapter that details borrower profiles and loan features. These include HECM loan purposes (such as home purchases versus refinancing of existing debt), payment plan options, interest rate types, borrower ages and maximum claim amounts and initial draws by recent borrower cohorts.

The agency emphasizes that its actuaries model HECM cash flows separately from forward mortgages and explicitly stress-test the reverse portfolio under varying home price appreciation scenarios.

Home price appreciation assumptions affect multiple levers across the program — including the available equity at the end of the loan, the size of recoveries through property sales and the loss severity tied to claims. Indirectly, home price growth can also impact payoff incentives.

The report notes that waning price growth in 2026 had an “outsized negative impact” on HECM capital compared with forward mortgages. This underscores why even modest regional or national home price corrections are more consequential for HMBS investors and issuers than for traditional mortgage-backed securities.

The stand-alone capital ratio of 5.43% for the HECM portfolio suggests that FHA still has room to absorb stress, but far less cushion than in the prior three years when the ratio ranged between roughly 16% and 25%. It also may create more difficulty for industry advocates in their push to reduce upfront mortgage insurance premiums.

In September, Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley told RMD that the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with the current mortgage insurance structure for FHA single-family loans and reverse mortgages. Gormley’s comments prompted pushback from NRMLA, which said it would continue to “dialogue with them around more risk-based pricing.”

An industry professional who was granted anonymity was more blunt in calling for lower premiums.

“The reality is this, if a client has to pay 2% to obtain the right to draw up to 30% of their home’s value, they will seek out other options,” the source said. “It should come as no surprise that HEIs and HEAs have been popping up everywhere. Even the gains on the proprietary side are the result of FHA’s inaction. Clients would rather accrue 10% interest annually to a lender than pay 2% upfront to a government insurer.”

The FHA report’s policy section does not identify any major new structural changes to the HECM program, but it does highlight several items of operational relevance.

This includes contract funding reallocation for assigned HECM property preservation expenses. FHA mentions a reallocation of contract funding tied to property preservation on assigned HECM collateral. While it’s a technical issue, it could affect vendors and servicers who manage preservation and conveyance on properties with HECM balances that are acquired by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

Fraud detection, data analytics and remediation were also mentioned. These areas are not limited to the HECM portfolio and apply across FHA single-family programs. Given the growing population of senior borrowers and the history of consumer protection scrutiny for reverse mortgages, these efforts may lead to tighter oversight of origination practices and borrower counseling outcomes in the HECM channel.

FHA also discussed ongoing system modernization efforts, including those tied to FHA Catalyst modules and uniform appraisal data initiatives. Over time, the report explained, better data capturing should improve the accuracy of HECM-backed property valuations — a key driver of assignment timing and loss estimates — and could result in more precise disclosures for HMBS investors.

The report also placed attention on the new permanent loss-mitigation waterfall for FHA forward mortgages that went into effect at the end of 2025. While that waterfall does not directly apply to HECMs, it signals a broader effort by the agency to standardize workout options and reduce cycles of repeated defaults. This approach could inform any future redesign of default resolution frameworks for reverse mortgages.

#5335. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5334. UP Fintech: Q3 Net Income Rises 16.4% QoQ, Client Assets Reach Record US$64.8 Billion

NEW YORK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- UP Fintech Holding Limited (Nasdaq: TIGR) ("UP Fintech" or the "Company"), announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. In the third quarter, the Company reported a revenue of US$172.6 million. Non-GAAP net income attributable to UP Fintech shareholders was US$49.9 million, up 16.4% QoQ and marking the second-highest quarterly result in the Company's history. During the quarter, the Company added 48,500 funded clients, up 48.9% QoQ and 54.1% YoY. Total funded clients increased 11.4% YoY to 1.364 million. Supported by strong net asset inflows, total client assets rose 6.7% QoQ to a record US$64.8 billion.

The Company was named one of the world's top fintech companies in the "Wealth Technology â Neobrokers" category for 2026 by CNBC and data analytics firm Statista, the second consecutive year the Company has appeared on the list.

Mr. Wu Tianhua, Founder and CEO of UP Fintech, said: "In the third quarter, we continued to advance our global growth strategy. New funded clients rose by roughly 50% both QoQ and YoY, led by Singapore and Hong Kong. Hong Kong stood out, contributing nearly US$1 billion in net asset inflowsâa new quarterly recordâwhile client assets grew more than 20% QoQ. Client assets also increased across all our international markets, underscoring the continued trust global investors place in our platform."

"We continued to broaden market access and extend trading hours, giving investors greater flexibility. Building on our 24/5 US stock trading service, we recently became one of the first online brokers globally to offer extended-hours trading in eligible US equity options. Orders are routed directly to US options exchanges, allowing clients to adjust positions and manage risk outside regular trading hours. In December, we plan to support Nasdaq's new 23/5 trading for US stocks and ETFs from day one. As market structure evolves, we will build on our 24/5 trading foundation and continue enhancing our products and execution capabilities to strengthen our position as a gateway to US markets for global investors."

Singapore market strengthens its competitive position with prestigious recognition

In Singapore, trading activity remained strong in the third quarter, further reinforcing Tiger's competitive position in the local market. New funded clients nearly doubled QoQ, while total trading volume increased 47% YoY, reflecting the rapid expansion of the local client base and growing market appeal. Across products, trading volume in US stocks, US options and Singapore stocks increased 61%, 87% and 44% YoY, respectively, demonstrating steadily rising investor participation across both global and local markets. The Company's localized offerings also performed well. Tiger BOSS Debit Card spending reached a monthly record in September, with total card spending increasing 40% YoY. During the quarter, Tiger Brokers Singapore was named "Best Personal Investment Platform" at the Euromoney Awards for Excellence 2026, recognizing its product offering, service capabilities and market impact.

Hong Kong Net Inflows Hit Quarterly Record as Client Engagement Deepens

The Company delivered strong growth in Hong Kong during the third quarter. Net asset inflows approached US$1 billion, setting a new quarterly record. Total client assets increased 20% QoQ and nearly doubled YoY, reflecting stronger asset gathering and an expanding high-value client base. Total trading volume increased 102.6% YoY, with trading accounts up 78.7%. The Company continued to enhance its Hong Kong market data offering, upgrading Level 1 real-time streaming quotes for Hong Kong equities and making them available free of charge to investors worldwide. The Company also recently hosted its flagship offline event, Tiger Investment Festival, bringing together its digital platform and offline engagement to deliver a richer client experience and deepen its connection with the local investment community.

US, Australia and New Zealand Deliver Broad-Based Growth, Deepening Local Client Trust

In the US, TradeUP delivered strong growth in client assets and funding. Net asset inflows rose 437.4% YoY, total Assets Under Custody (AUC) increased 84% YoY, and average net funding per new client grew 58.3% QoQ. Options were the main driver of trading activity, with contracts traded up 48.7% QoQ amid rising client demand.

Client engagement also strengthened across Australia and New Zealand, as more local investors used the Company's platform to access global markets. In Australia, total trading volume increased 88.8% YoY, new margin accounts grew 40.3%, and margin account AUC rose 116.1%. In New Zealand, total orders increased 28% YoY, with Australian and Hong Kong stock orders up 54.4% and 46.7%, respectively, reflecting growing demand for cross-market investing.

US Options Trading Hours Expand; Overnight Activity Up Nearly 80% YoY

In the third quarter, UP Fintech generated US$63 million in commission revenue, while interest-related income reached US$85.5 million, up 12.5% YoY. During the quarter, the Company expanded its derivatives toolkit with the launch of an Options GEX Analytics hub, bringing together gamma exposure, trading volume, open interest and Max Pain data. These tools help investors better understand market positioning, identify key price levels and make more informed trading decisions. In Hong Kong, the Company introduced a rollover feature for Hong Kong stock options*, allowing users to switch quickly between near- and longer-dated contracts and making it easier to roll longer-term positions. In Singapore, the platform introduced odd-lot trading for local equities and Fill-or-Kill (FOK) orders, lowering the barrier to higher-priced stocks and giving investors greater flexibility. The Company also launched a dedicated Daily Leverage Certificates (DLC) section, accessible from the rankings page or by searching for "DLC".

The Company's US stock overnight trading activities remained robust in the third quarter, with overnight trading DARTs up 76.9% YoY, underscoring demand for access beyond regular market hours. The Company also recently extended trading hours for selected US single-stock options**, giving clients greater flexibility to trade outside the regular session.

Despite a moderation in Hong Kong's IPO market, strong growth in the Company's retail client base drove aggregate IPO subscription amount to over HK$172 billion in Q3, up 261% YoY and reflecting growing engagement among global investors.

Wealth Management Grows as HNW Client Base Expands

Market volatility and opportunities across asset classes continued to drive demand from high-net-worth investors for diversified portfolios, yield enhancement and professional asset management. Active wealth clients with at least US$1 million in assets increased 20.4% QoQ. Structured note trading volume reached a record US$385 million, up 168% YoY and setting a new high for the second consecutive quarter. Mutual fund AUC rose 14.2% QoQ, while assets managed under the Company's Hong Kong Type 9 license increased 262.5% YoY to US$540 million.

TradingFront's Turnkey Asset Management Platform (TAMP) also maintained solid momentum. Platform AUC doubled YoY, total accounts increased 42.1%, and Q3 structured product net sales rose 318.5% YoY. TradingFront also launched AI-powered customer service and introduced cross-currency cash and Vault-powered purchasing power trading. The new capabilities allow financial advisers to place client orders across stocks, ETFs, funds and regular investment plans, enabling more efficient management of multi-currency portfolios.

Investment Banking Completes 11 Hong Kong IPOs and Co-Leads the Largest US IPO by a China-Based Company YTD

UP Fintech generated US$24 million in other revenues in Q3, including investment banking and Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP) services. The Company completed 11 Hong Kong IPOs across AI, autonomous driving, robotics and semiconductors, alongside several A+H offerings. It also led QuantGroup's follow-on offeringâits first Hong Kong follow-on transaction as lead bankâand co-led Longdian Wason's IPO, the largest US IPO by a China-based company year to date.

The Company's ESOP platform, UponeShare, added 64 ESOP clients during the quarter, bringing the total number of companies served to 904. Notable new clients included ROKAE Robotics, Star Sports Medicine and SENASIC. SaaS revenue increased 99.2% YoY, while consulting revenue rose 71.9% YoY.

The Company also added 13 corporate account clients during the quarter, bringing the total to 561. New clients included Longsys, Transsion Holdings, Robotechnik, LDROBOT and Extreme Vision.

#5333. Beyond commission splits: How wellness benefits give brokerages a recruiting edge

Brokerages are expanding benefits aimed at agent well-being, from access to group-style PPO options to coaching on stress and resilience. Executives frame the programs as foundational support as market conditions remain uncertain heading into 2027.  AI Summary

By many estimations, real estate professionals are facing the most challenging housing market in recent memory in 2027. Unlike in the past, many will be doing so with access to more resources than ever designed to ensure they are feeling healthy, at the peak of their game and ready to tackle whatever the 2027 housing market throws at them.

This is because over the past year, several brokerages announced a variety of wellness programs and health insurance opportunities they are now offering to agents, who as independent contractors, typically do not have access to things like insurance through their brokerage.

Since the start of 2026, ENRG Realty, Compass International Holdings, Equity Union Real Estate and John R. Wood Properties have announced the launch of health insurance or wellness benefits initiatives.

“We were founded on Maslow Hierarchy of Needs, so health insurance fits right in with some of the core basic values that we need to provide to our agents so they can be successful and thrive,” Erinn Nobel, the co-founder and president of ENRG Realty and a HousingWire Woman of Influence award winner, said. “In order for our agents to function at a high level, they can’t be sitting at home worried about an illness or being able to pay their bills because they don’t have health coverage. It is a foundational offering and a benefit for us to be able to provide it for our agents.”

Nobel said that while some Realtor boards or associations offer health insurance, there is often just one policy option, something she experienced first hand after moving to Alaska from Washington state.

“It was great to be able to access insurance through our board, but there was only one plan, so you couldn’t shop around,” Nobel said. “It just didn’t sit well with me that my options were so limited.”

A similar experience with challenges accessing insurance for his family is also what inspired Harma Hartouni, the CEO of Equity Union Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, to begin providing his agents with access to group-style health coverage options, including a nationwide PPO network, through a partnership with Trident BPO.

When he approached the executive team about launching this initiative, Hartouni said they were a bit divided as to whether or not they should do this.

“Some thought the agents wouldn’t care, but some of our managers thought it was great,” Hartouni said. “Ultimately, our agents are our clients, and I knew that if these people were not healthy or not in a clear mindset in this challenging market, they would not function well.”

In the current uncertain economic environment, Hartouni added that the offering has also provided many agents, who previously had access to insurance through a spouse who lost their job, a level of peace of mind that they couldn’t previously provide.

“The consistent feedback from agents is that they are saving money and are able to see better doctors,” Hartouni said.

Nobel said she’s heard similar feedback from her agents. After rolling out the program, Nobel said she and her team received countless messages from agents saying thank you. Beyond better serving existing agents, Nobel said the program also helped ENRG Realty with agent recruitment.

“It has become an attraction magnet for us. Savvy agents that have been in the industry for a while are starting to really compare brokerages and look at what benefits they get from each brokerage and the different values they provide,” Nobel said. “If an agent already has access to health insurance through a spouse or partner, then this may not convey the same value as it would to a self-employed single mom who would love to have access to health care.”

Hartouni has also noticed the agent recruitment benefits of offering health insurance.

“The smart broker is looking for producing agents that are in the middle of their career, where they still have plenty of years left in the business to learn and grow, but have already begun to establish themselves,” he said. “But these agents often have families to think about and how can we help them have one less thing to worry about? We can provide them with access to health insurance.”

While John R. Wood Properties is not providing agents with access to health insurance, the brokerage recently announced it was providing its agents with access to individualized coaching focused on their personal well-being and professional development, through a partnership with HatchPath. Through the program, agents can gain access to coaching support across a wide range of areas including nutrition, stress management, mental resilience, leadership, career development and major life transitions.

“People are just so burn[ed] out in general and everybody is on edge from personal challenges, financial challenges, family challenges. I just thought what better way to support our people than to give them access to coaching,” Corey McCloskey, the president of John R. Wood Properties, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think a lot of us who run businesses have realized that you bring your whole self to work. You can’t just turn off what’s happening in your personal life when you walk into your office — it affects you whether you realize it or not.”

While still in the early stages of the rollout, McCloskey said she has seen her agents and staff use HatchPath coaching for help with everything from financial planning to fitness and overall physical wellness.

Although brokerages are continuing to face challenging housing market conditions and ever-tightening profit margins, these executives believe it’s important for brokerages to support their agents beyond just professional development.

“If we are encouraging people to be entrepreneurs, we have to support them and provide them some sort of value,” Nobel said. “Anytime we can offer a benefit that has real value to agents, we really look to do that because ultimately that is what we as a brokerage are supposed to do — provide value for our agents.”

Nobel added that she would encourage more brokerages to consider providing agents with access to health insurance.

“This is something that we need to be offering our agents in the world right now,” she said. “Offering insurance is what is best for our industry.”

McCloskey, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, shares a similar view.

“Knowing that not only us, but other companies are supporting agents as whole people, I think that will only serve to make our industry better,” she said. “The younger leaders coming into the industry have seen the toll this industry can take on someone who doesn’t take care of themselves. They want to do things differently, and I think we have an opportunity now that we’ve never had before where we can offer these sorts of things to people and really tell them how important they are to us.”

#5332. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5331. Bitcoin Price Crashes Below $62K: What Should You Do?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has fallen below $62,000 for the first time since early July, extending a brutal November selloff as institutional investors pull billions from the market. BTC touched $61,270 just now, before recovering slightly to trade around $61,700.

Bitcoin price has now lost more than 10% over seven days, with selling pressure spreading across equities, precious metals and other risk assets. Yesterday’s $582.3 million outflow from US spot Bitcoin ETFs added another blow, bringing November withdrawals close to $3.5 billion.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest single-day outflow since launching. The same session saw $727 million in crypto liquidations, with bullish traders absorbing most of the damage.

Institutional demand is weakening, leveraged buyers are being forced out, and the Federal Reserve’s increasingly hawkish outlook is making speculative assets less attractive.

Bitcoin is now approaching $60,000, a level that could determine if the correction finds a floor or develops into something uglier.

The ETF withdrawals are arguably the biggest concern for Bitcoin holders right now. Spot Bitcoin ETFs became an important source of institutional demand after launching in January 2024. Their buying helped absorb available supply and gave traditional investors a regulated route into the market.

That demand is now moving in the opposite direction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost more than $1.1 billion this week alone. November’s cumulative withdrawals have approached $3.5 billion.

The pressure extends beyond ETFs. Rising Treasury yields and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase in December have encouraged investors to reduce exposure to assets that offer no regular income.

Meanwhile, derivatives traders are taking heavy losses. CoinGlass data showed more than $700 million in liquidations across crypto markets over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for 86% of the total.

Bitcoin itself recorded nearly $202 million in liquidations, with bullish traders suffering the majority of forced closures.

This creates a difficult environment for buyers. Falling prices trigger liquidations, which create additional selling pressure and push prices lower. The reduction in open interest also suggests excessive leverage is being flushed from the market.

The immediate battle is around $60,000. Bitcoin needs to reclaim $62,000 and establish support above it before bulls can confidently argue that the latest breakdown was temporary.

Scenario 1: Bitcoin loses $60K and heads toward $58K or $53K.

This is the bearish outcome. A decisive break below $60,000 could trigger another wave of stop-loss orders and leveraged liquidations.

The next downside area sits around $58,000, while more aggressive technical projections point toward $53,700.

The daily chart offers little encouragement for bulls. Bitcoin trades below its major moving averages, while bearish momentum continues to dominate. A sustained recovery in ETF flows would become increasingly important to prevent further deterioration.

Scenario 2: Bitcoin stabilizes between $60K and $62K.

This would give buyers time to absorb available supply without immediately reversing the entire November decline.

The liquidation wave has already removed considerable leverage from the market. If ETF withdrawals begin slowing, Bitcoin could establish a trading range before attempting another recovery.

But sideways trading alone would not confirm a bottom. Buyers need to demonstrate that they can defend support through multiple sessions.

Scenario 3: Bitcoin reclaims $62K and launches a relief rally.

A recovery above $62,000 would provide the first meaningful sign that sellers are losing control. A move toward $65,000 would then become possible, followed by resistance around $68,000.

Consistent ETF inflows, improving market sentiment, and a weaker dollar would strengthen this scenario. Without those developments, any rebound risks becoming another opportunity for sellers to exit.

For existing holders, the decision depends heavily on their entry price, investment horizon, and exposure. Long-term holders who bought substantially below current prices have more room to withstand volatility. Selling simply because Bitcoin crossed a psychological threshold risks locking in profits or losses without knowing whether the broader investment thesis has changed.

However, investors holding leveraged positions face a different problem. Falling prices can trigger forced liquidations regardless of their long-term convictions. Reducing leverage and protecting available capital should take priority over waiting for a rebound.

For buyers, the temptation to buy the dip is understandable. Bitcoin is considerably cheaper than it was just weeks ago, but cheaper does not automatically mean undervalued.

Buying in stages rather than committing an entire allocation around $61,000 offers more flexibility if the market tests $58,000 or even $53,700.

Bitcoin price remains vulnerable to another leg down. The $60,000 level is no longer just a psychological milestone. It is where the next major battle between buyers and sellers will be fought.

#5329. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5328. AI agent provider Sierra closes $1.75B investment amid rapid revenue growth

Six months after its last funding round, artificial intelligence startup Sierra Technologies Inc. today announced that it has closed a $1.75 billion late-stage investment.

Greenoaks and Lightspeed led the Series F deal. They were joined by a group of returning backers that included Alphabet Inc.’s GV fund.

Sierra sells a set of cloud services that enables workers to create AI agents without writing code. The centerpiece of the suite is Ghostwriter, which can automatically generate agents based on user-provided prompts and files. A software team, for example, could upload a set of bug reports and request an agent that can automatically group them by problem type.

Ghostwriter checks the dataset that users upload for formatting errors before putting it to use. Once an agent is ready, the tool simulates user conversations to find potential bugs. Ghostwriter places particular emphasis on edge cases, unusual requests that can trip up an agent if they’re not addressed during development.

Sierra also offers a second development tool called Horizon. It can be used to create agents that automate time-consuming tasks. A marketing team could build an agent that monitors user interactions with a product page over several months, finds areas for improvement and automatically makes the necessary optimizations.

Sierra powers customers’ agents using more than a dozen large language models. Simple requests are sent to latency-optimized LLMs, while more complex queries are processed by pricier frontier models. Sierra says that it also uses several internally developed algorithms.

Customers can manage their AI projects using a third Sierra product called Agent Studio. According to the company, it includes over 40 connectors that enable agents to retrieve information from external systems. There’s also a tool for building custom connectors.

Agent Studio detects gaps in agents’ knowledge. Furthermore, it can automatically fix some of those gaps. The platform detects when a human support representative answers a customer inquiry that the help desk hasn’t encountered before and turns it into a knowledge base article. From there, agents can use the article to answer similar requests.

The studio also lends itself to certain other tasks. A collaboration feature enables multiple team members to review agent updates before they roll out to production. If a technical issue makes it past the review, developers can use a debugging tool to study what went wrong. The tool displays every single step of the workflow through which an agent processes prompts.

Rounding out Sierra’s product portfolio is an AI assistant called Explorer. It can proactively flag notable business events without a prompt and search through a company’s internal datasets. In some cases, it also generates business advice.

Sierra’s latest raise, its third in 14 months, comes a few weeks after its annualized revenue topped $400 million. The company disclosed at the time that it had added nearly half the sum over the preceding quarter. Its customer base now includes half the Fortune 50.

Sierra will reportedly use the new funding to enhance its product portfolio and hire more salespeople.

#5327. ABB helps scale industrial AI with world's first motor featuring built-in intelligence

ZURICH, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ABB today launched Intelleqtâ¢, the world's first low-voltage motor with intelligence integrated at the factory, designed to deliver real-time operational insights from its first rotation. Its open architecture enables customers across industries to connect motor data to their existing digital platforms while retaining full ownership of their data. By delivering equipment-level intelligence through a plug-and-play solution, Intelleqt helps companies build the data foundation needed to scale AI-driven operations.

Intelleqt arrives as industries increasingly seek to move artificial intelligence from pilot projects into core operations, with data quality and availability remaining among the main barriers to adoption. Industrial AI can deliver measurable value, but scaling its deployment remains challenging.

While 84 percent of manufacturers report benefits from artificial intelligence, only 20 percent of AI use cases have successfully scaled.1 At the same time, the equipment powering critical sectors such as data centers, water infrastructure and food production remains one of the largest untapped sources of operational intelligence.

More than 300 million motor-driven systems operate worldwide, accounting for 60 percent of industrial electricity demand2. Yet most are not connected to the digital technologies used to improve reliability, efficiency and performance. As electrification, automation and industrial AI accelerate, the $18 billion global IEC and NEMA low-voltage motor market is also positioned for further expansion.

"ABB's investment in research and development is always focused on solving real customer challenges," said Stefan Floeck, President of ABB's IEC Low Voltage Motors division. "The shift towards AI-driven operations is accelerating, yet most of the motors powering global industry do not generate data and remain invisible to the intelligence being built around them. ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is a world first that opens a new chapter in motor development, transforming motors from mechanical equipment into sources of real-time intelligence."

By turning motor data into actionable insights, ABB Intelleqt helps customers improve reliability, increase productivity and identify energy saving opportunities of 30 percent or more3. Early fault detection can reduce unplanned downtime by up to 50 percent4, helping industrial operators avoid failures costing up to $1.5 million per incident5. Factory-integrated sensing, edge computing and connectivity give customers access to these insights from day one.

ABB Intelleqt is the latest example of ABB's investment in artificial intelligence and digital technologies, bringing equipment-level intelligence to one of industry's most important and widely used assets while helping customers build the data foundation for the next generation of industrial AI.

Launched today at the SPS trade fair in Germany, ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is now entering a customer co-creation phase, working closely with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and end users to develop solutions tailored to their operational needs. A broader rollout is planned for 2027, initially focusing on markets in Europe, Japan, China and India.

ABB drives shared success with customers through innovation and customer-focused research and development. Drawing on more than 140 years of engineering expertise, ABB plans to invest 4.5 to 5.0 percent  of Group revenues in R&D to support the development of pioneering technologies such as ABB Intelleqt. In 2025, ABB invested $1.3 billion in R&D. The company has around 7,800 R&D employees across facilities in more than 30 countries on six continents, with approximately half focused on digital and software development. Since 2022, ABB's total R&D investment has increased by around 30 percent.

#5326. Cost cutting is not cost reduction; builders and trades face a test

Strategem estimates tariffs add $12,919 to a typical new home, while NAHB data shows combined construction inputs up 10.4% year over year. Builders are seeking concessions, but long-run savings may require operational fixes with trade partners.  AI Summary

A reliable estimate of the tariff burden on a typical newly built American home puts the cost at $12,919, or about $4.88 per square foot.

That is before accounting for broader inflation in construction labor, transportation, services and other inputs that homebuilders must absorb while trying to make their homes affordable to increasingly price-sensitive customers.

This informed baseline calculation of tariff impact at the new-home level, developed by homebuilding supply-chain consultancy Strategem through its Strategy Pulse Pro platform, updates the National Association of Home Builders‘ April 2025 builder-reported tariff-cost estimate of $10,900 to reflect subsequent trade-policy changes. The model distributes tariff exposure across 17 material categories, with hardware and fasteners, steel products, lumber, cabinets, windows and aluminum accounting for some of the highest estimated costs.

By its nature, Strategem’s tally is a modeled cost burden, not a direct measure of tariffs paid on every home or of the amount passed through to buyers.

Still, it illustrates a difficult dilemma for homebuilders, and one none of them can simply avoid: Costs imposed upstream cannot necessarily be recovered downstream. And in that downstream market, households increasingly lack the financial capacity or confidence to buy homes at the prices builders need to charge.

That predicament, predictable in a falling market, is a reflexive homebuilding firm response that reverberates through homebuilding’s wider ecosystem like a bad-trip flashback. Homebuilders are looking to their suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and trade contractors to shoulder more of the financial pain.

It’s a law of dismal science physics during a downturn: Wringing a bit of margin improvement by most builders means squeezing suppliers’ margins into further negative territory.

The danger is that some builders may, and often do, push their business partners beyond what they can reasonably absorb. This tactic, seductive as it may seem as a way to claw back input cost reductions, mostly serves as a temporary fix. Ultimately, such quick fixes undermine the very production capacity, service reliability, and competitive supplier pools they will need to survive the downturn and recover.

Homebuilders have spent much of the past two years using price reductions, mortgage-rate buydowns and other incentives to preserve sales velocity. Those concessions have helped sustain production, but they have also eroded the earnings cushion – the “shock absorber” – that previously allowed many builders to absorb rising costs without substantially disrupting operations.

The squeeze is occurring on both sides of builders’ income statements. According to NAHB’s November 13 analysis of Producer Price Index data, goods used in new residential construction rose 9.8% year over year in October, while service inputs increased 11.3%. The combined input index rose 10.4%, including a 5.8% increase in building-material prices.

These are input-price indexes, not equivalent percentage increases in the total cost of constructing a house. Still, they reveal why slowing demand has not delivered the broad-based cost relief builders might otherwise expect.

The pressure is particularly difficult for smaller builders and suppliers with limited financial reserves. They must keep enough business flowing to cover fixed costs while protecting the margins and working capital required to remain viable.

Ken Pinto, a longtime homebuilding strategic-sourcing executive and co-founder of Strategem, and a friend of The Builder’s Daily, believes the industry risks conflating two fundamentally different types of cost reduction.

Purchasing departments are reporting savings from increasingly competitive bidding, he says, but those reductions often come from suppliers sacrificing profitability rather than from lasting improvements in how homes are built.

“When you reduce costs by going out to bid, going out to bid, going out to bid, you’re not taking cost out of the supply chain; you’re taking margins out,” Pinto says.

This self-preservatory instinct among homebuilding business decision-makers has important, potentially risky, consequences. A trade contractor who accepts a lower price to keep crews working may provide immediate relief to a builder’s direct costs, but the underlying costs of labor, transportation, insurance, equipment, and materials may remain unchanged.

When demand eventually recovers, those concessions may disappear. More troubling, some suppliers may not survive long enough to participate in the recovery.

Pinto points to manufacturers facing higher costs for steel, copper and resin-based products while struggling to secure corresponding price increases. Their customers may be able to delay accepting price increases, but the underlying costs do not disappear simply because builders refuse to pay them. The resulting margin compression can become unsustainable.

Conversations with homebuilding purchasing professionals suggest that the opportunities for further reductions vary considerably by category. Some material suppliers remain willing to compete aggressively for market share, particularly in areas where slower construction activity has created excess capacity. But trade contractors face different circumstances.

Years of declining production volume have already weakened some local subcontractor businesses. In some markets, established trade firms have closed, while others struggle with cash flow, payment disputes and mechanics’ liens.

At the same time, immigration enforcement has reduced labor availability in trades including framing, concrete, masonry, roofing, electrical work and painting. The result is an increasingly uneven marketplace in which a builder may find materials readily available but struggle to secure the skilled labor required to install them.

Residential construction also faces growing competition for certain resources from the extraordinary investment flowing into artificial intelligence infrastructure and data-center construction.

That competition is particularly acute in markets where large commercial projects – especially of note in Texas and Virginia ­– require concrete, electrical equipment, transportation capacity and specialized labor. Although residential and data-center construction workforces are not interchangeable, competition for certain services and materials can raise costs even as homebuilding activity slows.

The risk extends into 2027. A contractor with too little work today may be unable to retain skilled crews until demand improves. A builder who pushes that contractor’s prices below sustainable levels may find the contractor has disappeared, downsized, or committed its remaining capacity elsewhere when new-home orders return.

That is not merely a supplier problem. It becomes a builder’s problem across the construction cycle, quality, customer service, and profitability.

Pinto argues that builders and trade contractors have a much larger opportunity to improve profitability by jointly addressing avoidable operating costs.

One recurring example is construction scheduling. When a subcontractor arrives at a jobsite that is not ready, the contractor incurs labor, transportation and administrative costs without productive work. Unreliable schedules make it harder to allocate crews, while late changes, rework and unnecessary return visits consume resources neither party can afford to waste.

“We still get subcontractors showing up to job sites, and the job’s not ready for them. So, a dry run. This shouldn’t be happening,” Pinto says.

Consider the contrasting approach between 1. a homebuilder demanding a 5% reduction in a trade contractor’s bid and 2. the two businesses collaborating to eliminate repeated crew mobilizations, incomplete jobsite preparation and avoidable rework.

The first approach may reduce the builder’s invoice while leaving the contractor’s expenses unchanged. The second can reduce the actual cost of completing the work, creating room for both companies to improve their economics.

Achieving these operational efficiencies becomes especially important when homebuilding’s lower production volumes should give operating teams more opportunity to coordinate schedules, standardize specifications and eliminate recurring inefficiencies.

Pinto is developing a collaborative workshop, Tearing Down the Walls, with former subcontractor and Builderbeast Consulting founder Don Bronchick and industry colleague Andrew Stevens. The workshop’s premise is that builders and trade contractors can improve their economics by jointly examining the processes that create unnecessary costs.

The approach requires both parties to share information, acknowledge their contributions to inefficiency, and agree on measurable improvements. That is more demanding than threatening to award a contract to the lowest bidder, but it offers the possibility of savings that endure through a market recovery.

Homebuilding’s consolidation wave adds another dimension to the challenge. Larger builders have gained substantial purchasing leverage, but their long-term returns increasingly depend on integrating local operating expertise, supplier relationships and construction capabilities to build more effective enterprises.

The purchasing organization offering the lowest quoted prices does not necessarily lead to the lowest completed-home costs. A supplier who consistently meets schedules, maintains qualified crews, resolves field problems quickly, and supports a builder through fluctuations in demand may be worth more than the nominal difference between competing bids.

That does not excuse poor performance or prevent builders from replacing suppliers who cannot meet reasonable cost, quality, or service requirements. Competitive bidding remains necessary, and some vendors may still have room to lower their prices.

The key question is whether builders understand and choose between extracting a concession and improving the economics of the entire production process.

For 2027, the choice to improve holistic economics should guide purchasing and operating decisions. Builders need to understand which costs suppliers can control, which are driven by external forces, and which stem from the builder’s own practices. They also need to evaluate suppliers’ financial health, preserve alternative sources of capacity where practical, and measure total installed costs rather than purchase prices alone.

These measures will not close the affordability gap or restore lost homebuyer demand. Nor can they fully offset tariffs, higher financing costs, or skilled-worker shortages. They can, however, prevent homebuilders from worsening their operating position while trying to protect near-term margins.

Homebuilding companies have every reason to ask their business partners to share the burden of a difficult market. But there is a meaningful difference between sharing that burden and transferring it to a partner with no capacity to absorb it. Business leaders know the difference.

They know the ones best positioned for recovery may not be those that extract the deepest concessions today. They know that the real, more structural solution – and one that should keep most valued partner relationships intact – reduces the actual cost of producing homes while preserving the trust and transparency, skills and productive capacity that will allow them to build profitably when customers return.

That’s not to say it’s the easier, softer way forward, but when demand finally strengthens, a homebuilder will need more than an order backlog and available lots. That team will need capable partners still willing – and able – to build the homes. And they know it.
