#5325. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5324. Raleigh’s housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds

Pew reports Raleigh’s post COVID zoning reforms helped add 16,884 homes from 2021 to 2024. The city’s supply growth coincided with slower rent gains and a 15% inflation adjusted rent decline from 2022 to 2025.  AI Summary

For years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing. New research from The Pew Charitable Trusts shows what happened when Raleigh, N.C., followed that playbook.

Following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found. The result was a building boom, particularly for the townhomes and apartments the city’s earlier rules constrained. This uptick in homebuilding made renting more affordable in North Carolina’s capital city, especially for middle-income households and younger residents.

The report highlights how adding new housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minn., and Austin, Texas. The same dynamic is playing out across the Sun Belt, where many of the nation’s fastest-growing metros also have some of the loosest zoning rules, and where rents and home prices have dropped more dramatically than anywhere else in the country.

Raleigh didn’t rely on a single fix to make building housing easier. Its reforms combined a rewrite of its form-based code, an end to parking minimums, denser building near transit and a housing bond to support affordable housing.

“Of all of the drivers of housing costs – population growth, an influx of high-income earners, high land costs and high construction costs – we have the most agency and direct control over restrictive zoning regulations,” Patrick Young, Raleigh’s planning and development director, said in a statement.

Raleigh’s 2021 zoning reform, which expanded the city’s already-established form-based code, opened the door to more “missing middle” housing. It did so by replacing units-per-acre caps with physical standards such as lot size, yards, and building height.

The changes legalized duplexes, triplexes and quadplexes in more residential districts and expanded where townhomes can be built. Under the new form-based code, further refined in 2022, builders can now construct small apartment buildings and tiny houses with up to two dwelling units on compact infill lots.

As a result, builders can now construct missing middle housing in more of Raleigh’s neighborhoods, a shift that Pew links to better affordability for middle-income and younger residents.

Raleigh eliminated its citywide parking minimums in 2022. That allowed developers to fit more housing units on each property and, in some cases, spared them the expense of building costly parking structures, which can often make a project too costly to pursue.

The city also spurred housing growth by allowing taller, denser buildings near major transit corridors. Transit Overlay District zones allowed for an extra story along Bus Rapid Transit corridors, extending half a mile along some local bus routes.

Additionally, a density bonus allows developers to exceed height limits by up to 50% if at least 20% of the extra units are designated as affordable, below-market units.

The City of Raleigh approved an $80 million housing bond in 2020 that is projected to create at least 700 affordable homes, fund homebuyer assistance and help homeowners with home repairs.

About $14 million has already gone to four developments totaling more than 240 units, while another $24 million in gap financing will back over 470 additional units, more than 90% of which will be affordable to households earning 60% of area median income or less.

Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh added 16,884 housing units, growing its housing stock by 7.7%, even as the city’s population grew by 5.8% over the same period. Raleigh’s housing growth also outpaced the state (5.7%) and national (3.2%) rates during that period.

Of the 16,884 units added, roughly 2,000, or 12%, were affordable to households earning 80% or less of area median income (AMI), with Raleigh’s housing bond funds helping support their development. Density bonuses contributed about 200 of those affordable units, accounting for 10% of the total.

Additionally, Raleigh’s code changes intentionally shifted a large share of production away from detached single-family homes toward townhomes, duplexes and tiny homes. Since 2021, the city has issued more than twice as many townhouse permits as in 2015 to 2020, and has permitted more than 200 duplex units and over 200 accessory dwelling units (ADUs).

As a result, average monthly rents rose at only half the national pace and fell in real, inflation-adjusted terms. Pew’s analysis estimates inflation-adjusted rents declined 15% from 2022 to 2025, and, as of 2025, the income needed to afford the city’s median rent dropped from 79% of AMI to 65%.

Raleigh’s experience mirrors a wider trend among fast-growing Sun Belt markets, where less restrictive zoning and fewer barriers to housing development have supported greater housing production and helped moderate housing costs. The South accounted for more than half of all U.S. housing starts between 2021 and 2025, while Sun Belt markets continue to lead the nation in rent and home price declines.

According to Yardi Matrix’s October 2026 multifamily report, rents fell year over year in 12 major US markets. The Sun Belt accounted for ten of those, led by Austin, Houston, Nashville, Tampa and Phoenix. The for-sale market shows a similar pattern, with home prices dropping disproportionately in the Sun Belt while climbing in the Northeast and Midwest.

#5322. Grab your GeekWire Gala early bird tickets now, and party Dec. 10 with Seattle’s tech community

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 18, 2026 at 1:38 pm

Everyone loves a holiday deal, and this week is a good chance to take advantage of one: early bird pricing ends this Friday for tickets to the 2026 GeekWire Gala.

Seattle tech’s biggest holiday celebration takes place Dec. 10. We’ve got a new venue and fresh experiences, and it’s a great chance to rub shoulders with hundreds of the region’s top founders, investors, entrepreneurs and business leaders.

The party is moving this year to The Shop, an exclusive venue in Seattle’s SoDo neighborhood featuring an extraordinary collection of classic and exotic cars that should help rev up the festivities.

The GeekWire Gala features food and drink, signature cocktails, games, music, dancing and more. Part reunion and part networking extravaganza, it’s a chance to turn our holiday party into your holiday party. Bring your friends, colleagues, clients, or entire team.

We’re also excited to bring back our Uncommon Thinkers program, recognizing the creative minds and unconventional builders shaping the future of the Pacific Northwest. Presented in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners, the program shines a spotlight on innovators making a difference across our region.

In partnership with Microsoft, we’ll also be raising awareness this year for six amazing nonprofits that help make our region a better place to live.

The festivities take place Thursday, Dec. 10, with the main event running from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. at The Shop at 2233 6th Ave. S. in SoDo.

Dress to impress, break out your holiday flair, or keep it geek chic. Cocktail attire is welcome, but there are no fashion rules at this party.

A big thank you to our returning presenting sponsor, First Tech Federal Credit Union, and our 2026 sponsors, including Microsoft, Wilson Sonsini, Zoox, University of Washington, ALLtech, Accenture, WTIA, Turkish Airlines, Washington State University and Prime Team Partners. We’re also grateful to Greater Seattle Partners for its continued partnership on Uncommon Thinkers.

Sponsorships and group ticket packages are also available. Contact us at [email protected] for details.

The AWS re:Invent livestream runs November 29–December 3, so you can follow the week from wherever you are. Choose from 60+ sessions across topics and skill levels, from introductory overviews to advanced deep dives. Catch every major launch as it is announced. Customers share what they learned, and select sessions include live Q&A. Livestream registration is free.

#5321. Georgia builders give affordable housing an essential new identity

Georgia residential developers and builders are rebranding affordable housing as essential homes, aimed at workers like teachers and first responders. The effort is linked to policy priorities such as permit review accountability under SB 447 and changes to final plat and bonding.  AI Summary

Put an affordable housing project on a planning commission agenda, and the neighborhood naysayers come out of the woodwork to fight.

They argue it will destroy the neighborhood’s character. Labeling the development as workforce housing doesn’t help much.

What’s in a name? An affordable home – or neighborhood – by any other name is still affordable, no? Still, companies rebrand when the current brand is struggling. And Georgia homebuilders and land developers are taking a crack at giving “affordable housing” a brand makeover, one that’s less stigma and more economic and social fabric dynamism.

The Georgia Residential Land Development Council and the Home Builders Association teamed up to dub affordable housing “essential homes.” They are pairing it with a tagline: “Homes for the people who keep Georgia working.”

But defining essential homes as housing that workers can afford near where they work could be applied broadly as lawmakers from the federal to local levels wrestle with how to make housing more affordable.

“It’s a reality nationally that the buying power of the average American is not considered in land use and zoning policies,” Jay Knight, GRLDC’s chairman, told HousingWire TBD. “Essential homes for essential people intends to move the conversation from sticks and bricks allowed to the important people being prohibited.”

The definition names no home size or price point. It asks whether the people who work in a community can afford to live there. Teachers, firefighters, nurses, first responders, healthcare workers and skilled tradespeople are among the livelihoods the term “essential” captures best. They also include younger Georgians hoping to buy a first home.

Austin Hackney, HBAG’s executive vice president, said in a statement that the term puts a human face on the affordability debate. He said that when workers can’t find homes within reach of their income, the effects reach employers, schools and local businesses.

The rebrand comes with a policy push. The groups say zoning restrictions, long permit reviews, infrastructure requirements and delayed final plat approvals add substantial costs that end up in home prices.

GRLDC helped advance Senate Bill 447, which took effect July 1. The law sets timelines and accountability for Georgia’s land disturbance permit reviews. The council’s next target is final plat and bond reform. It wants reasonable approval timelines, standardized bonding requirements, and an end to delays that keep completed developments from moving forward.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development considers housing affordable when occupants pays no more than 30% of gross income on housing costs. Programs add other definitions, often tied to area median income. Affordable housing typically targets households at 60% of the area median income or less, while workforce housing covers roughly 60% to 120%.

Workforce housing, however, isn’t explicitly defined in federal law or regulation, according to a March 2026 Congressional Research Service analysis. But the term is used to avoid saying a housing development is affordable housing.

Opposition often centers on neighborhood character. Researchers also find residents may fear newcomers’ socioeconomic status more than the buildings themselves. Property values are another common worry, though research cited by the Florida Housing Coalition found almost no negative effect on neighboring market-rate homes.

Knight said the definition problem became clear at a speaking engagement. He asked a room of roughly 40 people to define affordable housing. One woman said Section 8. Someone else said anything under $400,000. A person from the Northeast thought it meant rent control.

Knight said that convinced him people weren’t talking about the same thing, which made the conversation unproductive. His business partner suggested essential homes. Knight said the organizations liked it immediately.

Terms such as affordable homes, starter homes, first-time buyer or workforce housing arrive with a definition already attached. Knight said “essential homes” encourages people to ask what it means, which gives the groups a chance to set the definition themselves.

The rationale behind the rebranding is that if local governments can dictate what can be built, the standard shouldn’t exceed what their own employees can buy. Knight said the average municipal employee earns about $60,000 to $62,000 a year in Georgia. That means they can afford about a $225,000 home.

In most U.S. markets today, that would buy roughly 1,100 square feet on a 35-foot detached lot, with no garage and no homeowners association, he said. He added that would put the price at about three and a half times annual income, close to the ratio GIs returning from World War II paid in the late 1940s and 1950s.

Knight said zoning conditions have pushed home prices to a much higher ratio. High-cost areas like California, New York and Florida are prime examples. In Silicon Valley, the median home price is 11.4 times median household income, according to an annual report from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. The Miami metro’s ratio is 7.6.

High prices relative to income are a major reason the median first-time homebuyer is now 40. It’s an all-time high, according to the National Association of Realtors. Such a disparity is why California and Florida have been at the forefront of housing reforms.

The Georgia campaign will put faces to the term: a police officer, a teacher, a nurse and a forklift operator. Knight said it will portray the kinds of workers that municipalities court with industry.

Knight, who sits on an advisory council for the National Association of Home Builders, said he has shared the term with the executive director of the Houston Home Builders Association. He said Houston is now discussing it, since builders nationwide are having the same conversations.

“Who can be against essential housing?” Knight said.

#5320. ABB helps scale industrial AI with world's first motor featuring built-in intelligence

ZURICH, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ABB today launched Intelleqtâ¢, the world's first low-voltage motor with intelligence integrated at the factory, designed to deliver real-time operational insights from its first rotation. Its open architecture enables customers across industries to connect motor data to their existing digital platforms while retaining full ownership of their data. By delivering equipment-level intelligence through a plug-and-play solution, Intelleqt helps companies build the data foundation needed to scale AI-driven operations.

Intelleqt arrives as industries increasingly seek to move artificial intelligence from pilot projects into core operations, with data quality and availability remaining among the main barriers to adoption. Industrial AI can deliver measurable value, but scaling its deployment remains challenging.

While 84 percent of manufacturers report benefits from artificial intelligence, only 20 percent of AI use cases have successfully scaled.1 At the same time, the equipment powering critical sectors such as data centers, water infrastructure and food production remains one of the largest untapped sources of operational intelligence.

More than 300 million motor-driven systems operate worldwide, accounting for 60 percent of industrial electricity demand2. Yet most are not connected to the digital technologies used to improve reliability, efficiency and performance. As electrification, automation and industrial AI accelerate, the $18 billion global IEC and NEMA low-voltage motor market is also positioned for further expansion.

"ABB's investment in research and development is always focused on solving real customer challenges," said Stefan Floeck, President of ABB's IEC Low Voltage Motors division. "The shift towards AI-driven operations is accelerating, yet most of the motors powering global industry do not generate data and remain invisible to the intelligence being built around them. ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is a world first that opens a new chapter in motor development, transforming motors from mechanical equipment into sources of real-time intelligence."

By turning motor data into actionable insights, ABB Intelleqt helps customers improve reliability, increase productivity and identify energy saving opportunities of 30 percent or more3. Early fault detection can reduce unplanned downtime by up to 50 percent4, helping industrial operators avoid failures costing up to $1.5 million per incident5. Factory-integrated sensing, edge computing and connectivity give customers access to these insights from day one.

ABB Intelleqt is the latest example of ABB's investment in artificial intelligence and digital technologies, bringing equipment-level intelligence to one of industry's most important and widely used assets while helping customers build the data foundation for the next generation of industrial AI.

Launched today at the SPS trade fair in Germany, ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is now entering a customer co-creation phase, working closely with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and end users to develop solutions tailored to their operational needs. A broader rollout is planned for 2027, initially focusing on markets in Europe, Japan, China and India.

ABB drives shared success with customers through innovation and customer-focused research and development. Drawing on more than 140 years of engineering expertise, ABB plans to invest 4.5 to 5.0 percent  of Group revenues in R&D to support the development of pioneering technologies such as ABB Intelleqt. In 2025, ABB invested $1.3 billion in R&D. The company has around 7,800 R&D employees across facilities in more than 30 countries on six continents, with approximately half focused on digital and software development. Since 2022, ABB's total R&D investment has increased by around 30 percent.

#5319. Anthropic’s Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline

Anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software. With a new update today, Claude now can tell developers when the code it has generated is ready to ship into production environments.

The company announced the launch of Claude Ship, which is a new suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals. The last one is the most interesting of those capabilities, because code reviews and fixes are nothing new for AI. But Claude’s ability to automatically approve code changes based on the policies predetermined by an organization’s developer team is a novel development that has not been seen before.

Claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the new bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools. At those organizations, fresh code is being whipped up in double-quick time, and there are also AI agents for checking that code and providing fixes if it’s not working as hoped. But until now, the final review and approval process has always been performed by humans. Claude Ship changes that.

The idea is that human developers can delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they’re asking AI to create.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line,” Anthropic said in a blog post. “But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code and we wanted everything after the pull request to move that fast too.”

Anthropic said Claude Ship consists of three parts. The first is Code Review, which is a tool that has been generally available for some time already. The other two are PR Steward and Claude Approvals, and they’re both still in beta.

PR Steward is designed to handle issues such as failing continuous integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After each push, it will leave comments on what changes were made and how to roll them back if necessary.

Once PR Steward is done, Claude Approvals takes over. It works by applying an approval policy that’s left as a file in the codebase’s repository. The approval process can incorporate various elements, including the findings in Code Review and the organization’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Anthropic is urging early adopters to be cautious. Because Claude Ship is still in beta, it recommends running Claude Approvals in observe-only mode first. It also advises teams to begin with just one repository first, and set monthly spending limits so they can maintain more control over everything.

#5318. The first price is the one nobody scores

Industry metrics focus on sale price vs final list price, but that can hide multiple reductions. With 21.2% of listings showing a price cut, the more useful CMA score is sale price vs the first asking price.   AI Summary

Agents are more confident in the comparative market analysis than they have been in years. In the 2026 Survey of Best Practices for CMAs and Listing Presentations, from Giant Steps Advisors in partnership with Lone Wolf Technologies, 89.6% of 2,165 real estate professionals said they expect CMAs to become more relevant, up from 67% in 2020. HousingWire reported on October 22 that the same respondents are ready to bring AI into the work, with 83.2% very or somewhat likely to use AI-assisted CMA tools, and suggested that the lasting value of the document may lie in explaining a price rather than producing one.

That is a fair reading of what a CMA does at the kitchen table. It is also an incomplete one, because it judges the document on a single day. The CMA is scored on whether it persuades the seller to sign. Whether the price it argued for held up once buyers began making offers is a question the industry has no standard way to answer.

The pressure on that single day is rising. Roughly two-thirds of agents in the survey named pricing as the leading seller objection, up from 52.7% in 2020, and 33.6% said they had lost a listing because they and the seller could not agree on a price.

At the same time, the survey found that 90.8% of respondents trust the MLS above any other source for comparable sales. Similar sources, increasingly similar tools and familiar formatting tend toward similar documents. When two agents arrive with reports that look alike, the seller is left choosing between two persuasions with nothing to say which one was right last time.

The industry does keep a score, but it is the wrong one for this purpose. In the National Association of Realtors 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers, the final sale price was a median of 99% of the final listing price. The final listing price is the one left standing after any reductions. A home listed too high, cut twice and then sold sits in that figure looking almost exact, because the comparison begins after the correction has already been made. Reductions are not unusual.

Redfin reported that 21.2% of listings carried a price cut in the four weeks to November 1, 2026. The figure that tells a seller how well a CMA priced their home is the sale price compared with the first asking price, but that is not the figure the industry reports.

Even the first asking price is not always the number the CMA stood behind. HousingWire’s October report noted research showing that about half of agents put a listing price in their CMA and about half do not. Where the price is left off the page, the CMA can never be checked against the outcome, because it never committed to a number in the first place.

The gap widens when agents move. HousingWire reported in March that roughly 230,000 agents moved to a new brokerage in 2025, according to Courted’s 2025 State of Brokerage Recruiting and Retention Report. The sale prices stay in the closed files after an agent leaves. The judgment that set the first prices, and the sense of where that judgment ran high or low, leaves with the agent.

None of this is an argument against AI in the CMA, or against the CMA as a persuasion tool. Persuasion is part of the job, and a seller deserves an agent who can explain a price clearly and defend it under pressure. The difficulty is that the explanation is examined closely on the day it is given, while the outcome arrives months later and is measured against a different number.

The industry has spent years making the valuation faster to produce and easier to present, and the survey suggests the next generation of tools will make it faster still. The question it has not yet asked is the one a seller would ask if they knew to: When this agent’s first prices met real buyers, how close did they come? Until someone asks it, every CMA will be judged on the day it persuades and never on the day the house sells.

Nikola Gojkovic is the founder of CMAflow and writes on residential valuation methodology.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5317. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5315. Reducing risk by protecting trust across the real estate transaction

An analysis of 668 reported wire fraud events found $123.8 million in exposure and $11.5 million in losses. About 79% of events were tied to participants outside a title company’s direct control, underscoring the need for shared verification across partners.  AI Summary

A secure lender platform cannot protect a buyer who acts on fraudulent instructions received through another participant’s email. An agent’s familiar name can make a message persuasive even when the agent has no authority to move funds. For mortgage, title and real estate professionals, those connections deserve a place in the fraud prevention conversation.

An analysis of 668 reported wire fraud events spanning a decade identified approximately $123.8 million in reported financial exposure and approximately $11.5 million in documented losses. The findings point to a practical concern for everyone involved in a transaction: protecting an organization’s systems addresses only part of the risk.

We examine what those reported events suggest about trust, why participants outside the funding process matter and how organizations can strengthen verification across business relationships.

Approximately 79% of reported events, 78% of reported exposure and 80% of documented losses were associated with participants operating outside the title company’s direct control. Of the 668 events reviewed, 57 resulted in documented financial loss.

These figures describe the reported events analyzed. They should not be treated as an industry-wide loss rate or as proof that risk has shifted over time. Association with an external participant also does not, by itself, establish where an account was compromised or who was responsible for a loss.

The concentration nevertheless raises an important business question. If a fraudulent request gains credibility through a customer, agent, attorney or other participant, will the next organization in the transaction recognize and verify it before someone acts?

The traditional approach to fraud prevention focuses on authority. Organizations identify who can move money, approve payments, authorize disbursements or initiate wire transfers and then build controls around those functions.

That remains necessary. But an attacker may also seek access to someone who influences the person sending money. Transaction details, familiar correspondence and knowledge of an approaching closing can help a fraudulent message appear credible without access to the lender’s or settlement provider’s systems.

Residential real estate transactions are particularly susceptible to this type of manipulation because they depend on trust at every stage of the process. Buyers trust agents. Sellers trust agents. Consumers trust lenders. All parties trust the professionals coordinating the transaction. Most participants are communicating with several unfamiliar parties while simultaneously navigating a process that is complex, time-sensitive and financially significant.

For a consumer, a request that appears to come from a familiar professional may feel like part of that process. Fraud prevention must help customers distinguish a trusted relationship from a verified instruction.

Mortgage lenders, title companies, brokerages and independent professionals operate with different resources and security practices. A participant may use an email account without the monitoring or administrative oversight available within a larger organization. That difference creates a coordination challenge, not a reason to assign blame.

An agent may understand the buyer’s timeline and concerns better than anyone else. A loan officer may be the person the buyer calls when a request seems confusing. A settlement professional may be the first to see that expected funds have not arrived. Each has an opportunity to reinforce safe behavior at a different point.

The strongest internal controls lose some of their value when customers receive inconsistent guidance about who will provide instructions, how to verify them or where to report a suspicious message. Those expectations should be established before the closing deadline makes every request feel urgent.

Lenders, agents and settlement providers should explain their respective roles early. Identify who will provide wiring instructions and how the customer should independently confirm them. Reinforce that guidance as closing approaches rather than relying on a single warning in an email signature.

Before acting on wire instructions, confirm them directly with the appropriate party using a previously established, independently verified phone number. Do not rely on a phone number supplied in the message you are trying to verify.

Replying to the same email thread is not sufficient because an attacker may control the account. Question unexpected changes and escalate unusual requests through your organization’s established procedures before money moves.

Awareness efforts should reach loan officers, agents, transaction coordinators and customer-facing staff, as well as employees authorized to disburse funds. Training should explain how a routine message or introduction can influence a consumer’s decision to trust instructions.

Strong email security, multifactor authentication, employee training, monitoring and incident response capabilities remain essential. Broader coordination adds to those protections. It does not reduce the need to secure accounts and systems within each business.

Organizations should identify whom to contact when instructions appear suspicious or expected funds do not arrive. Staff should know how to pause their part of the transaction, involve the appropriate settlement and lending contacts and activate established fraud response procedures. Customers need a clear way to raise concerns without feeling that they are creating an inconvenience.

The difference between reported exposure and documented loss in the analysis is substantial. It is consistent with the value of verification and intervention, but the totals alone do not establish which controls prevented losses or explain every event’s outcome.

Organizations can learn more by reviewing their own near misses. Where did a questionable request enter the process? Who recognized it? Was the customer able to reach the right person? Did a partner’s instructions conflict with the organization’s guidance? Those questions turn an avoided loss into an opportunity to improve the next transaction.

Wire fraud prevention is a shared responsibility across mortgage lending, title and settlement services and real estate. A participant does not need authority over funds to influence where those funds go.

The practical response is to make verification part of the customer experience from the beginning. Clear roles, consistent guidance and accessible escalation help people act safely when a familiar name or urgent request makes fraud difficult to recognize.

Successful fraud prevention frequently occurs because someone slows down, asks an additional question and verifies information before money moves.

Bruce Phillips is the SVP and Chief Information Security Officer at MyHome, a Williston Financial Group Company™.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5314. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/19 to correct that Charlie Trillingham worked for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business, not the Foster School itself.

#5311. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5310. XRP Price Prediction: $1 Wall Breaks, What’s Next?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP price has lost the $1 mark, and buyers are running out of powder to defend the breakdown. The token floats at $0.95, extending a painful decline that has erased 28% of its value over the past month. XRP has now closed below $1 for six consecutive sessions, turning a psychological support level into an immediate resistance.

The next important test sits around $0.89, where buyers previously stepped in during November’s sell-off. A break below that level could expose $0.80, leaving XRP vulnerable to another leg lower.

Institutional demand has offered little immediate relief. U.S. spot XRP ETFs recorded $19.13 million in weekly net outflows through November 13, their largest weekly withdrawal in eight months. The selling has since cooled, with ETF flows showing no net movement on November 18 and 19. Cumulative inflows remain around $1.79 billion.

CryptoQuant data shows Binance’s XRP Supply Shortage Index climbing to 2.4 on November 19, its highest reading since July. Whale withdrawals reportedly exceeded $127 million since November 10.

Exchange supply is tightening, but that hasn’t translated into buying pressure; sellers are continuing to control price action.

XRP isn’t the only project betting on blockchain utility to attract the next wave of capital. Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is taking a different route, building an SVM-powered Layer 2 designed to bring faster transactions, lower fees, and smart contracts to Bitcoin.

The idea is to unlock Bitcoin-linked liquidity for DeFi, decentralized applications, and potentially tokenized assets without relying on Bitcoin’s slower base-layer execution. Its testnet wallet, bridge, and explorer are already available for community testing.

The presale has raised more than $33.2 million, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136877 and advertised staking rewards of 35% APY. November 26 is the planned token launch and presale deadline, leaving little time before the current entry window closes.

XRP’s daily Relative Strength Index has fallen below 30, placing the token firmly in oversold territory. However, that alone won’t stop the downtrend.

The immediate support zone sits between $0.94 and $0.95. Losing this area would put the November 14 low near $0.89 back in focus.

A decisive break below $0.89 could open the door toward $0.80.

On the upside, XRP needs to reclaim $0.985 before challenging the psychological $1 barrier again. A sustained move above $1 would give buyers their first meaningful opportunity to reverse the breakdown.

For now, the bearish structure remains intact. XRP needs more than an oversold bounce to convince buyers that the worst is over.

#5309. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5308. Valona launches Deep Research Agent for competitive and market intelligence

The agent researches competitors and industries in advance, giving enterprise strategy and intelligence teams deeper, source-backed answers to complex market and competitor questions.

HELSINKI, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Valona Intelligence has launched its Deep Research Agent, placing agentic research at the core of its competitive and market intelligence platform. The agent prepares and regularly refreshes analyses of competitor investments, industry developments and emerging risks.

Which competitors are adding capacity, and where? What do their investments and outlooks reveal about where the market is heading? Which risks are emerging? Answering these questions requires piecing together numerous sources, often across companies, markets and languages. When teams research the same questions independently, they risk duplicating work and reaching different conclusions from different sources.

The Valona Deep Research Agent builds on curated, continuously monitored industry intelligence, including specialist and local-language publications, company disclosures and structured company data. Unlike general-purpose AI research tools, where source selection can vary between investigations, Valona provides a consistent, industry-specific foundation for research. The agent uses this foundation to investigate recurring questions in advance and keeps that research current, so answers go deeper and every finding links to its source.

"Our customers' most important questions are rarely answered by one source or one search," said Stuart Reynish, Chief Product Officer at Valona Intelligence. "Our Deep Research Agent does the heavy lifting before the question is asked, drawing on sources selected for our customers' industries. When a strategy team asks where competitors are expanding or what is changing in its market, they can build on research that has already brought together the relevant evidence, rather than starting from scratch."

The agent's first research became available to customers on 30 October 2026. It addresses recurring questions such as where competitors are adding production capacity, what management teams expect from the market, how companies are performing financially, and which external risks and opportunities are shaping an industry. In the first two weeks, Valona's AI features drew on the new research and financial data more than 13,000 times.

Valona Deep Research Agent will continue expanding with new industry-specific analyses. Planned developments include direct customer access to the Deep Research Agent for investigations on demand, alongside agentic workflow automation for creating intelligence deliverables and managing ongoing market and competitor monitoring.

To see Valona Deep Research in action visit valonaintelligence.com.

Valona helps strategy and intelligence teams at more than 500 global enterprises move from reacting to market and competitive change to anticipating it, with source-backed intelligence that supports strategic decisions on where to compete, where to grow and where to invest. #5307. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5306. Amazon acquires key assets of AI startup Decart for reported $7.5B

Amazon.com Inc. today announced plans to hire the technical staff of startup Decart.AI Inc. and acquire its core technology.

The company didn’t disclose the terms of the deal. However, sources told Bloomberg that Amazon is paying about $7.5 billion. That’s nearly twice the valuation Decart reportedly received after its most recent funding round in May.

In August, reports emerged that the company had drawn takeover interest from Anthropic PBC. The artificial intelligence provider reportedly sought to buy Decart for $6 billion but walked away from the deal in September. Rumors that Amazon could swoop in emerged the following month.

Decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf will join the tech giant along with Decart’s research team. Additionally, Amazon is acquiring the technology behind the company’s DOS platform, which helps boost the efficiency of AI models. Decart claims that the software can reduce the cost of some neural networks by a hundredfold.

The company hasn’t shared detailed information about how DOS works. However, the blog post in which Decart announced its May funding round did reveal that the platform optimizes AI models by “tuning the kernels.”

Kernels are the basic building blocks of neural networks. They’re relatively simple code snippets designed to run across a large number of chip cores. One common approach to optimizing them, kernel fusion, combines multiple kernels into a single code snippet that uses less hardware. In July, Decart disclosed that a custom model it had developed with DOS uses kernel fusion.

The company says that the platform also includes “proprietary compilers.” AI compilers translate neural networks into the platform-specific programming language of the host chip. They also optimize the models along they way. For example, the compiler that Amazon Web Services offers for its AWS Trainium machine learning chip uses quantization to compress models into a more memory-efficient form.

It’s unclear whether Decart positions DOS as an alternative to the default compilers provided with AI accelerators. According to Amazon, Decart has “worked closely” with its engineers since 2025 to optimize the performance of workloads deployed on its Trainium chips. The newest commercially available iteration of the chip, Tranium3, provides 2.52 petaflops of performance when processing FP8 data.

Amazon stated that the acquisition will help “further optimize both its inference and custom silicon performance.” According to the company, the goal is to not only speed up customers’ models but also lower their cost.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”

The acquisition doesn’t include Decart’s portfolio of internally developed AI models. Its two newest algorithms, Lucy 2.5 and Oasis 3, are world models that generate virtual environments based on prompts. The former algorithm is optimized for low-latency content creation, while the latter is designed to generate training data for robots.

#5304. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.
